A magnetoelectric theta-term represents a topological component in the action of an axion insulator, exhibiting several time-reversal symmetry breaking phenomena collectively referred to as the topological magnetoelectric effect (TME). Our research explores the physical characteristics of the magnetoelectric theta-term by demonstrating its association with a topologically nontrivial topological magnetoelectric reaction and the Witten effect, alongside the topological Hall effect stemming from the anomaly half-integer quantum Hall effect. We establish a unified framework for analyzing these phenomena and show that the quantized topological magnetoelectric and Witten effects serve as clear indicators of the topological nature of the system under consideration.

In complex systems characterized by redundancy, the propagation of minor disturbances is a crucial factor. Typically, this redundancy is discarded as the system becomes more intricate, assuming linear growth or saturation of the disturbance. What if, however, the system's non-linearity and time delays could instead exponentially accelerate the spread? Our research reveals that modulating time delays in non-linear systems with a single delay line can lead to dramatic increases in the dispersion of trajectories from their starting points.

This study introduces an extensive interpretation of a probabilistic lambda calculus. Building on existing global interpretations for non-probabilistic languages, this work adapts this approach to incorporate probability. A new framework is developed to evaluate the convergence of probabilistic computations without relying on specific transition system criteria. This technical report also examines the applicability of these global interpretations to weak and strong beta-reduction strategies and proves that they are both sound and complete with respect to contextual equivalence.

This study presents a novel, automated design mining method that utilizes natural language inputs to extract design decisions and processes from online discussion archives, such as GitHub. The approach is validated by examining its conclusions over time, revealing both the diversity and evolution of design choices within a software community. The data shows that software communities frequently revisit and revise past design choices, often due to emerging requirements or limitations. Understanding the stability of designs offers insights into their quality and enables more accurate prediction of long-term success. To achieve this, we developed a design mining pipeline that parses natural language discussions to reconstruct the context, participants, and options presented, and then evaluates the choices made according to specified criteria. For a more thorough evaluation, the study incorporates human validation to compare the quality of designs selected by the system and developers manually. The results demonstrate that our system accurately identifies and organizes both early-stage and long-term designs, and the study provides valuable insights into the effectiveness of design choices.

Our research validates the holographic principle and pinpoints the source of gravity. A previously unresolved issue in quantum field theory has also been addressed - the origin of mass. Mass arises from the same mechanism that generates the mass of elementary particles via the Higgs mechanism but caustically, post-the electroweak phase transition as the universe cooled. A globally coherent field now fills all space, influencing local fluctuations of the field through the gravitational interaction, manifesting as we perceive it. Our model also addresses the hierarchy problem, the dark matter issue, and proposes that black holes are composed of post-expansion quantum coherence. Holes are comprised of coherently locked particles with no internal structure, observed from the outside as a defect in the Higgs field, viewed from the inside as a massless Goldstone boson with infinite coherence. Holes are comprised of coherently locked particles with no internal structure, viewed from the outside as a defect in the Higgs field, and, viewed from the inside, as a massless Goldstone boson with infinite coherence.

Non-smooth optimization problems can be effectively tackled using established techniques such as proximal-gradient methods. Nonetheless, we argue that we should not overlook the increasing body of knowledge in differential geometry and the advancements in geodesic optimization techniques that have been making an impact on the resolution of problems occurring naturally in problems formulated on surfaces. Our goal is to demonstrate how the concept of exponential mapping provides a reliable transformation for converting nonsmooth optimization problems set on surfaces into problems with fixed surfaces, thereby allowing the application of Newton acceleration methods. Specifically, we show the feasibility of implementing geometric proximal-point and accelerated proximal-gradient algorithms for solving problems on surfaces, resulting in linear convergence and global optimality.

In a commutative ring with identity, a ideal I is considered feebly 1-absorbing prime if for any ideals I1, I2, and I3 within the ring, the product of I1, I2, and I3 is contained within I, then either the product of I1 and I3 is contained within I, or I2 contains a element that when multiplied with an element of I3, it becomes contained within I. Building upon previous research, this paper examines feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals in non-commutative rings.

The new data for $\bar B \to \rho \ell \nu_\ell$ decays ($\ell=e,\mu$) produced by PEP-II are introduced. Utilizing a sample containing 1.509 billion $e^+e^-$ collisions at the $\psi(3770)$ resonance, occurring at 10.58 GeV, researchers identified 4200 signal candidates after accounting for 2440 background events. This analysis incorporated both fully and partially reconstructed $B$ decays featuring hadronic decays of the opposing $B$ meson to enhance missing momentum resolution and separate signal from background. Measurements yielded the branching ratios for $e$ and $\mu$ decays as $(8.546\pm0.203\pm0.046\pm0.096)\times10^{-4}$ and $(8.408\pm0.194\pm0.044\pm0.094)\times10^{-4}$ respectively, with uncertainties stemming from statistical, theoretical and Lattice QCD considerations. Results demonstrate agreement with the existing data for $\bar B$ decays into $\rho$ particles with leptons and neutrons. Additionally, ratios for $e$ and $\mu$ partial reconstruction were computed across multiple kinematic dimensions. These findings include findings related to forward-backward asymmetry and lepton flavor univers

As sensitive surveys scan the skies, the resulting massive databases of low-resolution spectra are limited by the inherent constraints of traditional spectroscopy.  These constraints can be over come by custom engineered solutions, namely photonic devices, which can isolate and individually examine narrow sections of light.  By exploiting the precise control of light within an integrated chip, these photonic devices can precisely target individual wavelengths of light with high accuracy and efficiency.  By collecting a comprehensive set of these targeted spectra, the full shape of a celestial object's spectrum can be reconstructed with greater detail and fidelity, ultimately yielding a more detailed and comprehensive understanding of the cosmos.  By refining cross-matching techniques through massive photonic data sets, the accuracy of astronomical research can be significantly elevated, ultimately leading to groundbreaking discoveries about the universe.

Evaluating medication pairs is a complex task that's crucial for analyzing a wide range of electronic health record data. The interplay of multiple factors including treatments, individual differences, and concurrent medications makes identifying accurate drug interactions a challenging task for both humans and machines. To tackle this issue, we have developed RDL4M2P, a Relational Deep Learning framework for medication pair evaluation, which leverages graph-based models to capture essential insights from patient records. Our approach utilizes a sophisticated entity-relationship network that incorporates multiple entity types and their interactions, enabling us to uncover subtle and interconnected patterns in medication evaluation. In particular, we showcase how our model effectively identifies a known statin and concurrent drug interaction, while also how clinical experts leverage an interactive system to verify their expertise and catch imbalances, such as a patient's inconsistent blood type.

Maintaining healthy roads is a top priority for transportation agencies and their failure to do so has a far-reaching impact on the transportation sector. Currently, there is no efficient approach in place for detecting substandard roads, especially in underdeveloped areas, due to the absence of an established system for road harm identification. A recent advancement in deep learning has shown promise in identifying road damages but each nation typically employs an independent road harm identification system, due to the varied nature of road surfaces, traffic conditions, and vehicles, resulting in an expensive and time-consuming process. In an attempt to bridge this gap, transfer learning has been introduced, allowing models trained in one country to be utilized in another, thereby reducing costs associated with multiple independent road harm identification studies. This research assesses the feasibility of transferring knowledge between datasets collected in different countries, specifically between South Korea and India, and analyzes the effect of data imbalance on classification performance. Moreover, the study explores the effectiveness of data augmentation in addressing this issue and presents the outcomes of experiments conducted using datasets from both nations.

Reinforcement learning tasks with partial observability are notoriously difficult to solve. In many cases, agents must rely on hidden representations of observed data, learned through extensive training, to achieve better results. However, this reliance introduces a multitude of unsupervised objectives, making it challenging to pinpoint the most effective guidance for generating effective representations. In this paper, we investigate an alternative approach where agents can mimic the behavior of successful agents in a different environment, accessible in the form of demonstrations. This Cross-domain Mimicry from Observations (CMO) paradigm requires demonstrations in a simple, two-dimensional visual space and does not depend on the successful agent's underlying reasoning process. Our study shows that CMO significantly outperforms existing methods for solving complex partial observability tasks, such as navigation and object manipulation, despite only having access to demonstrations in a much simpler, two-dimensional version of the environment. This demonstrates the potential of CMO for solving highly challenging reinforcement learning tasks with only a small amount of relevant demonstrations available.

This study investigates association rules with confidence above 100%, which are
relevant for data analysis purposes. It explores the concept of redundancy in
association rule sets, which are redundant if they exceed a minimum cardinality.
We examine various redundancy removal techniques for association rule sets and
focus on those that retain all data associations. The research provides a definition
for minimal-base association rule sets, which are compact representations that capture
all data associations. We also discuss the concept of minimal-size association rule sets,
which represent associations most efficiently, and show that they are always redundant.
A new algorithm is proposed to identify the smallest possible association rule sets.

A mandatory therapy system has been implemented in Spanish prisons since 2009. 
This context offers a natural experiment opportunity to study the effects of compulsory therapy on incarcerated individuals' mental health. 
We've conducted a natural experiment to examine the effects of this policy by analyzing data from the 2007 census. 
Our findings reveal that the compulsory therapy system leads to significant improvements in incarcerated individuals' mental health, while also yielding positive external outcomes. 
The size of these improvements in mental health indicators amounts to 0.20 and 0.15 standard deviations, equating to 25-30% of the overall distribution. 
Moreover, we've observed that the positive impacts on mental health translate into a decrease in violent recidivism rates and a substantial reduction in violent re-offending by 57% and 68%. 
We've also detected heterogeneity in the size of these effects, which we explain through the compulsory therapy system's emphasis on specific therapeutic approaches. 
This explanation offers further insight into the operational mechanisms of compulsory therapy systems and policy design.

The purpose of this paper is to explore various types of Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials and their unique properties in relation to the broader category of Apostol-type Bernoulli polynomials. We derive recurrence relationships for the newly defined polynomials which enable us to establish equations related to their corresponding infinite series. Additionally, we present the corresponding generalizations as matrices.

This study explores the concept of radio monitoring using autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles and theoretical chart estimations. We analyze the precision of spectrum examination and develop an algorithm to estimate theoretical charts in environments with minimal sensor density. The research leverages the principles of Gaussian fields and derives mathematical expressions for estimation uncertainty and convergence rates. A theoretical framework is created for radio monitoring systems operated by UAVs, incorporating constraints on communication range, energy efficiency, and network connectivity. We utilize geometric probability theory to assess monitoring coverage and network stability. Finally, we validate our findings through simulations on theoretical and real data sets, demonstrating estimation reliability in building radius regions.

This research introduces a novel HMM-based anomaly detection technique for multivariate systems by monitoring individual and collective behavior of system components through scalar metrics. The proposed method examines the likelihood of observed gauge data using an established Hidden Markov Model framework, allowing for the detection of anomalies in real-time. Specifically, our anomaly detection system is applied to a multivariate continuous caster, where each process step is represented by a single indicator variable. The results show that the method effectively identifies equipment malfunctions, with a significant improvement in fault detection rate and a substantial reduction in false positives compared to a conventional HMM-based approach.

This research proposes a comprehensive individual verification system that utilizes audio-visual-thermal sensors. The system integrates visual, auditory, and thermal modes, with visual and auditory components occurring simultaneously, and thermal component following immediately after. Visual and auditory data are gathered using a network camera with specific resolutions, and the thermal image is extracted by processing the red, green, and blue channels from the RGB camera. All sensor data are then analyzed using deep learning techniques before being incorporated into a verification model utilizing SMOTE and Deep Ensemble methods. The proposed system demonstrates an exceptional accuracy rate of 99.95% on the CASIA-FV40 dataset.

Recent research has shown that enhancing training data with minimal work can lead to significant improvements in the performance of automatic speech recognition and machine translation. While a variety of data augmentation techniques exist, they often rely on the assumption that an audio signal can be manipulated in a meaningful way, which is not the case for information itself. In this paper, we argue that the focus should shift from "synthesizing more data" to "consuming more information." To that end, we propose a new minimal effort data enhancement technique that systematically varies the timing of words in speech inputs. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated by the substantial performance gains it achieves on the Kit and LibriTTS-2 datasets for keyword spotting, automatic speech recognition, and machine translation tasks, often outperforming existing augmentation methods by a significant margin and at a lower computational cost.

For any positive integer n, the average of its maximum likelihood estimates for the blending parameters π is shown to be biased. Specifically, the bias is calculated as (π̂π̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂̂

A new framework for safeguarding individual privacy was formulated by Murtagh et al. in their 2020 proposal for the Fuzzy Differential Privacy standard, representing an extension of traditional differential privacy concepts. This framework accommodates situations where an adversary's assumptions about an individual's attributes are interdependent, unlike prior models that treated adversary assumptions as independent. In this paper, we examine the limitations of a specific disclosure avoidance mechanism, known as randomized response, for continuous data sets under one-sided differential privacy constraints. Our analysis reveals that this mechanism is incapable of meeting these constraints when the adversary's assumptions are interdependent. To overcome this disclosure limitation, we suggest an algorithm that utilizes the Laplace distribution to modify each individual's reported characteristics before they are released. This method is then evaluated for its effectiveness in meeting one-sided $\epsilon$-differential privacy requirements under various adversary assumptions that depend on multiple variables. Notably, our findings show that even when the adversary's assumptions are interdependent, this algorithm can provide significant privacy benefits compared to standard disclosure avoidance mechanisms.

We conducted an analysis of a recently discovered gas gap in the disk surrounding the young star AS 209, which has a similar structure to that around HR 2547. The gap, primarily composed of solid particles, contains a central void with a diameter of approximately 18-24 astronomical units and contains very little gas. The gas within the inner region of the disk has a surface density 5 to 10 times lower than expected. This unusual structure presents two possible explanations: either the gas within the void has turned into solids or the gases within the inner disk have migrated outward. While migration seems to be less likely, it's possible that small molecules like CO, H2O, and H2 have simply moved outward without entirely leaving the void. However, it's more likely that the void consists of larger and heavier particulates, and that the void's width is defined by the position where the solids begin to settle onto the floor of the void.

This paper proposes an evaluation framework for time-stamped data, presenting a diverse set of tools and methods to analyze such data from multiple perspectives. Our approach and toolkits/libraries enable the computation of standard and advanced evaluation metrics for various time-stamped evaluation settings, including online and batch evaluations with or without labeling, and multi-label computations. The effectiveness of our evaluation suite is demonstrated through its application in multiple domains and settings, with detailed toolkits and libraries available for use.

The concept of average field game models with control restrictions and state constraints is examined, with criteria established for determining when smooth profiles of state distributions satisfy existence and characterization problems. It is shown that under these games, smooth profiles can be achieved through gentle strategies. A precedent example is shown to be resolved by introducing a new, smooth profile, thereby resolving an outstanding problem.

Recent analyses using large-scale surveys have drawn attention to the possibility of an elongated structure composed of stars within the Milky Way. Distinguishing this feature from the disk and bulge regions using color is complicated by the presence of variable stars, which can skew the overall color. Researchers addressed this issue by applying a series of filters to isolate variable stars and examine the remaining stellar distribution in color space. Although some features persisted, the overall pattern disappeared when the variable stars were removed or removed data was simulated using random selection. These findings suggest that the feature may not represent a distinct, physically-bound object, but could instead be the result of data bias or artificial effects. To further investigate, researchers plan to analyze the spatial distribution of the stars involved and compare it to the galaxy's overall map.

Producing high-quality clothing requires maintaining a consistent design language across different garments to create a distinct and cohesive brand identity. Visualizing the full range of an apparel collection helps identify inconsistent designs that require adjustment to maintain a unified aesthetic. We introduce a new task, consistency detection, to identify visual inconsistencies within a collection of clothes by suggesting low consistency images for user selection. To achieve this, we develop a novel model, VICTOR, which contrasts pairs of clothing based on their consistency levels. Given the lack of labeled data for this task, we incorporate fashion-oriented contrastive pre-training, which pre-labels clothing with stylistic attributes and trains the model to perform consistency detection. Experimentally, our proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art performance, and our pre-training strategy effectively adapts the model to our target task using only self-supervised learning. Furthermore, our approach outperforms a baseline method in the consistency detection task.

The coherence of non-classical light sources has been the subject of debate, with some researchers arguing for a decoherence model that attributes their uniqueness to partial coherences in the transverse mode. This perspective frames the non-classical states as exceptions to the general rule of classical coherence. Contrarily, asset theories propose that non-classical features arise from the absence of certain classical properties. This perspective gains traction due to potential advantages in quantum information processing applications. In this work, a comprehensive asset theory is presented, encompassing the Schrödinger, Heisenberg, and phase space representations of quantum mechanics to define the essence of non-classical light.

Achieving efficient model training across multiple devices is a major challenge. The Federated Learning approach addresses this challenge by coordinating a centralized server that collects gradients from devices, aggregates them periodically, and sends the updated model back to the devices. To synchronize all devices during training. the server waits for their reports. This leads to slower learning as devices with faster hardware progress ahead of the others. This study demonstrates that this synchronization issue arises because devices follow the same learning path. By making the paths of different devices independent of one another. it becomes possible to speed up the training process. The authors introduce a method to achieve this independence and compare its effects on device synchronization. Additionally, they explore how this independence affects the device's model performance and present experiments validating these findings.

This study researchs a joint operational calculus within the algebra of polynomial functions, a subset of the larger space of tempered distributions. We derive specific formulas for function transformations and derive an expansion of a joint polynomial function in terms of generalized Hermite series. Furthermore, this study derives a set of differential equations that the generalized Hermite series satisfies.

The dimension of the Marshland and the dark matter's primary component, which comprises the majority, has led to the conclusion that it should be denoted as 'O'. Our research posits that the dark matter's O-dimensional fraction consists primarily of primordial black holes. Employing the Longstanding Hierarchy Model to analyze the universe, we find strong evidence that supports the existence of Primordial Black Holes as the main source of dark matter, and that the O-dimensional Marshland serves as the foundation for generating water and heavy elements.

Scientific experiments have shown that soap and lemon oil coatings on floating objects exhibit elastic properties, making them suitable for further study into their coating thickness. When the container is vigorously shaken, the floating objects coalesce and exhibit complex behavior, resulting in the emergence of patterns, including distinct regions bordered by unique types of matter coatings, and eventually, cracks in these elastic layers. To understand the dynamics of these cracks, we model the coating as a thin layer of material on heavy substrates, similar to heavy car tires. The heavy rollers prevent the coating from buckling when compressed but facilitate a specific type of failure, specifically transverse fractures. The relationship between the distance between cracks, their orientation, and factors, including surface tension and adhesion forces, is derived from a theoretical model and finds support in scientific observations. The theory suggests that a specific type of fracture occurs when a compressive force surpasses a critical shear threshold, resulting in the separation of the substrate and the release of the substrates' attached portion into the surrounding fluid. The comparison between the theoretical predictions and experimental findings shows a strong correlation, demonstrating the accuracy of the theoretical model.

We suggest a method to enhance the conductivity of GaN, which has excellent material properties. By forming a nanolayer with specific crystal orientations and integrating it with either ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ at the c-axis interface, we discovered enhanced anisotropic strain effects on the GaN electronic structure using first-principles calculations. These findings indicate that compressive strain increases the effective hole mobility within the GaN nanolayer, potentially offering a feasible solution to GaN's high-resistivity challenge in optoelectronic applications, which GaN is widely used in, such as light-emitting diodes, lasers, and microelectrode array biopotential detection systems.

Ultimately, our research paves the way for oop LED emission while leveraging ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ as novel, effective materials for engineering anisotropic strain effects in semiconductors.

Achieving wide-ranging navigation in the ocean requires marine robots to move from one known location to another, but existing location data is often fragmented and scattered. To overcome this issue, a new method is proposed that uses a revised version of Gaussian Process Regression to work with discontinuous and uneven data sets. The approach involves redefining the regression problem for multiple output values, introducing the concept of virtual data to fill in the gaps, and applying a sparsification technique to improve efficiency. The results show that this new method outperforms traditional approaches by producing more accurate predictions and reducing computation time. The proposed method was tested on a marine robot and successfully enabled navigation across various locations using collected data.

We've found new formulas expressing the modified isothermal coordinates of surfaces after the application of Darboux and Calapso transformations, which we've proven are isometries for their induced metrics. The relationship between the isometric properties of the Darboux transformation and the Pickinann-Riemann-Schilf theorem has also been explored. The development of our result was motivated by an analysis of isometric transformations shared by both the Darboux and Calapso transformations, which we've found to be related to the $\eta$-transform introduced by Montiel and Ros. The $\eta$-transform arises from a combination of two functions, one being a lift to the 3-sphere and the other a function on the 2-sphere, that preserve the first fundamental form of a surface.

We investigate the minimal smoothness required for nonparametric regression functions to ensure that their estimators converge at an optimal rate. By considering a regression model with a regressor and an error term drawn from specific probability distributions, with the conditional expectation function falling within a certain function space, denoted as $\mathcal{S}_d$, this rate can be determined. The function space $\mathcal{S}_d$ encompasses functions whose expectations, when multiplied by any polynomial of degree $d$, remain square-integrable, and thus includes $\mathcal{S}_0$, functions whose values converge as their arguments approach the boundary of the domain. This research provides rates of convergence for two widely used nonparametric estimators: the kernel and series estimators. The results reveal that the kernel estimator may not always achieve the optimal rate, despite being consistently as the bandwidth and the sample size converge. To address this limitation, the performance of the kernel estimator can be significantly improved by applying a boundary correction. By considering two distinct approaches to the kernel function, these corrections can be implemented, and the resulting estimators exhibit asymptotically negligible biases. The performance of the estimators is evaluated through their mean-integrated squared error and their finite sample properties are examined through simulations.

The $\lambda$-version of r-Stirling numbers of the second kind, denoted by $S_n^{(r)}(\lambda)$, can be defined as the coefficient of $x^{\underline{n}}$ in the falling factorial system with degree $n$. This paper presents and proves multiple identities related to $\lambda$-version of r-Stirling numbers of the second kind.

Temporal knowledge tracing aims to determine how students acquire new knowledge over time, based on their interactions with temporal educational data. Traditionally, machine learning connections are established based on item features and labels; non-stationary models are typically required to account for concept drift, which occurs when the importance of items changes over time. These models are resource-intensive and complex. Our study explores the possibility of using fixed models, commonly employed in natural language processing, for concept drift in temporal educational data. We assess the effectiveness of these models based on their predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and robustness to concept drift, comparing them with current state-of-the-art non-stationary models. Our research reveals that certain types of fixed models used in natural language processing can outperform non-stationary models in addressing concept drift, suggesting that the consideration of item features may not always be necessary.

We establish that the C*-algebras associated with any two finite directed graphs are shift equivalent if and only if their associated C*-algebras are strong shift equivalent through an algebra with properties of a ring and star operation. This finding generalizes the existing concept of strong equivalence for finite graphs to graphs that may have graphs whose out-degrees are infinite. This robust shift equivalence in graphs corresponds to a specific type of equivalence in finite algebraic matrices, thus answering a long-standing question posed by Williams. This equivalence also extends to non-finite graphs, allowing us to classify these graphs based on their associated C*-algebras and a specific finite algebraic matrix.

We are examining how a strong magnetic field impacts the interaction between two particles, specifically within the context of Quark-Gluon Plasma, by using a general theoretical framework for the propagator and solving equations based on the Dyson-Schwinger equation in a specific theoretical framework, known as the Landau gauge. Our study reveals that the influence of two distinct interactions leads to different outcomes for the anisotropic behavior of the particle pair, but the external magnetic field has a significant impact on this anisotropic behavior. Furthermore, the low-momentum particle region is significantly affected by the external magnetic field, resulting in confinement at this low-momentum region. Our results also indicate that the external magnetic field increases the intensity of the interaction at the lowest momentum point of the compact region, while its effect on the higher momentum points is varying, depending on the interaction's characteristics. Our data also indicate that the external magnetic field has a suppressing effect on the interaction at a specific range of momentum, known as the intermediate momentum range, by analyzing the spectral density of the interaction, known as the Oscar function. Our analysis also indicates that at a specific range of momentum, known as the high-momentum range, the interaction's intensity increases more slowly with the external magnetic field compared to the intermediate-momentum range.

Inferred knowledge from a graph can be expressed as a first-order logic formula, which can then be used to determine whether models of natural language can correctly apply this reasoning to answer questions. To date, no opportunities existed to train the model on the results of this reasoning process. Our study involves creating a dataset where the model must answer questions that require inferential answers, and then fine-tuning the model to bridge the gap between raw logical output and the required answer format. By fine-tuning, the model is able to converge on the correct answers, and this converging process is stable and effective, yielding improved performance in two evaluated tasks: answering questions about narrative and inquiry answers. Our results show that the model's capabilities are largely influenced by two factors: the level of reasoning and the extent to which the supporting evidence is evident in the given context. Our study demonstrates that pre-trained language models' ability to perform reasoning can be enhanced through supervised training, and our approach offers initial insights into the types of reasoning these models are capable of executing independently of fine-tuning.

We introduce two novel hierarchies of multilinear expansions, known as multilinear Fourier and Radon-Nikodym expansions, which provide comprehensive decompositions in high-dimensional spaces. These expansions build upon existing theories and have significant applications, such as the 'influence' concept utilized in computer science to analyze algorithms' sensitivity to high-dimensional inputs. Furthermore, we apply these expansions and a novel multilinear Bourgain's lemma to resolve a longstanding conjecture regarding the scalar $L_1$ multilinear embedding conjecture, as well as an integrative conjecture proposed by Gharibvand and Santhanam.

This paper investigates the effectiveness of prompts in selecting tasks without prior exposure to them, a novel approach that utilizes prompts to identify tasks most aligned with an agent's strengths, even in the absence of any preceding experience with the new task. We evaluate this method across two distinct reinforcement learning environments, comparing it to alternative approaches like task-conditional models and agent-conditional frameworks, highlighting the pivotal role of prompts in fine-tuned task selection.

This article provides a more general framework for $\mathscr L$-invariants, expanding upon existing work by Imai-Ikeda and Glanois. Building on Iwasawa theory's class field theory foundations, we adopt Artin L-functions and their associated representations as the basis for an expanded concept of $\mathscr L$-invariants. This new framework integrates the prior research of Iwasawa, Imaki-Ikeda and Glanois into a unified theory. As a result, we obtain more comprehensive results for specific cases, including a more in-depth calculation of an idele class character for a biquadratic extension. This new framework is motivated by the study of biquadratic extensions, and we incorporate the relevant work on Imada-Ikeda as special instances.

In atomic quantum information processing, microwave field detection using Rydberg atoms offers high sensitivity and has proven effective in detecting single microwave photons. Nevertheless, simultaneous detection of multiple frequencies at the atom using traditional methods is technically difficult. We have developed a novel machine learning-based approach that allows the discrimination of multiple Rydberg states based on the simultaneous induction of various frequency transitions by a single microwave pulse. This innovation enables the parallel analysis of a complex microwave signal at the atom. We have demonstrated the feasibility of this method in experiments with three different cesium atoms exhibiting distinct frequency transitions. The use of computer simulation and neural network analysis allows us to determine the identity of different Rydberg states induced by a microwave pulse on the atom. This innovation has the potential to expand the capacity of atomic quantum systems by increasing the number of qubits or enabling the application to other atomic species.

The ultra-diffuse galaxy UGC 8838 is undergoing a collision with a smaller galaxy, and they are in the process of merging.  Scientists studied a distinct, ring-like feature in a image of UGC 8838 using computer simulations.  They discovered that the ring has a stable edge, similar to a sharp line, and used this information to estimate the mass of the ring's central black hole to be around 40,000 to 400,000 times the mass of the sun.  They found that the ring's shape can be understood through simple physics and that the ring's features suggest a black hole at its center.  They concluded that the ring will continue to provide valuable information about the black hole in the center and that the ring's stability is a unique state that can be understood through the same model used to study other spiral galaxies.

This dissertation investigates various measures of complexity within the study of quaseregular mappings. Initially, it establishes the correct definition and properties of Hausdorff dimension for these mappings, correcting a previously erroneous definition by P\"{o}hltz. Subsequent research focuses on determining whether certain topological properties, such as the Hausdorff dimension or separability, of the Julia set in quasiregular mappings correspond to those of the underlying space. Employing techniques like Riemann surface composition and Kelvin's inversion, the dissertation provides examples demonstrating that the Hausdorff dimension and separability of the Julia set can differ from the values defined by the underlying space's dimension. Nevertheless, under the condition where a quasiregular mapping's degree equals one, the underlying space's separability is reflected in the Julia set's separability. To expand our understanding of the dynamics within quasiregular mappings, the dissertation also examines the density and distribution of periodic points in these mappings. Utilising the dimension of the Julia set and applying methods from quasiconformal theory, the dissertation presents conditions under which the set of non-recurring wandering points occupies either negligible measure or constitutes a substantial portion of the phase space. Additionally, the dissertation considers the set of non-recurrent points associated with quasiregular version of the Holomorphic Shilov boundary theorem.

Using data from MGS, ODY, MRO and MAVEN missions, the frequency and spatial distribution of gravity waves in the Martian atmosphere were analyzed. A significant overlap was found in the thermosphere frequency range across the four missions. A notable feature was the lack of a midlatitude boundary in the waves' vertical distribution. A thorough comparison was carried out with model simulations and a substantial variation in the waves' amplitude was found at altitudes above the nominal ionopause. A thorough understanding of the governing physical processes is necessary to explain this phenomenon. A thorough comparison of the temporal and spatial distribution of the waves among the four missions revealed similarities in their distribution patterns. A theoretical explanation of this similarity was proposed within the framework of linear stability theory.

A comprehensive study of Nu-Nu and nucleus-lepton interactions at the LHC was undertaken using the ALICE detector at a $\mathit{\sqrt{s_{\mathit{N\mathit{N}}}}}$ of 5.02 TeV during a full LHC run. This paper provides current progress in measuring UPG interactions via J/$\mathit{\psi}$ mesons, specifically Nu-Nu $\mathit{\gamma}\mathit{\gamma}$ production in Pb-Pb experiments. Preliminary results from ALICE demonstrate that Pb-Pb UP collisions can be distinguished from central collisions via the rapidity distribution of the J/$\mathit{\psi}$ in 2015 and 2018 data sets. The results are analyzed using both perturbative and nonperturbative QED models, which may aid in understanding the evolution of the Pb nucleus's charge distribution. Additionally, a framework to measure the lead ion's root-mean-square radius in Pb-Pb UP collisions was developed through the $\mathit{\gamma}\mathit{\psi}$ invariant mass and rapidity distributions. This framework revealed that the calculated number of J/$\mathit{\psi}$ pairs aligns with theoretical predictions based on a Landau model for Pb-Pb collisions.

A robotsketcher controls its sound output with audio feedback, which it interprets as an collaborative partner in the creative process. Initial interactions are turn-based, as the sketcher creates visual shapes, then deletes them to make space for new ones, and the audio output reacts in response to both actions. Over time, the sketcher learns to think ahead to create desired sounds, and the partnership evolves into a more dynamic collaboration, with the audio output becoming an integral part of the creative process.

The application of recurrent neural networks to sequence-based tasks has been
extensively studied in the literature. This report begins by offering a clear and
comprehensive overview of recurrent neural network designs, suitable for beginners
or those seeking to update their knowledge. It then delves into the vital aspects
of training recurrent models, including the issues of long-term dependency and the
computational demands associated with sequential processing. These key points are
then used as a framework for the classification of various recurrent models, each
described in detail.

To effectively combat health crises like epidemics, it is crucial to make optimal decisions promptly.  However, formulating these decisions in a precise and universal manner is challenging due to multiple factors, including financial considerations, travel restrictions, and time limits.  By developing a precise solution that addresses these constraints, decision-makers can realize the highest possible benefit by balancing health safety and economic stability.  A study involving decision-makers and modelers of disease spread has created a precise evolutionary game theory model to simulate various interventions' impacts on both health and economics.  The model takes into account decision-makers' preferences, information about disease spread, and social welfare concerns, as well as factors like hospital capacity, medical resource availability, and economic losses.  Analyzing the model using evolutionary stable strategies and a game-theoretic decision-making tool called GMPC has revealed that precise social distancing decisions, made in real-time, can yield the highest combined benefit for decision-makers and the economy. The decision-makers' payoffs and the model's precision payoffs are aligned and converge as models improve.

End-to-End (E2E) Machine Learning (ML) workflows have become ubiquitous, 
encompassing diverse applications such as ImageNet classification and SharedTask 
Challenges on platforms like Kaggle. These E2E pipelines require the joint 
operation of multiple software tools, each with its own associated learning 
objectives and performance metrics, resulting in a complex network of 
dependencies. This interplay of dependencies poses significant challenges for 
data troubleshooting. Disentangling the effects of data issues across this 
dependent network is particularly demanding, necessitating the development of 
effective significance measures for each data sample. This paper reevaluates the 
notion of significance through the lens of Shapley values and our experiments 
reveal that these values offer superior discriminative accuracy in locating data 
problems compared to existing methods. Moreover, these Shapley significance 
values exhibit adaptability to various troubleshooting scenarios, including 
subsequent model retraining with updated data.

This text highlights how modern enumerative geometry draws upon statistics, combinatorics, and topology to address unresolved queries. By presenting itself as a narrative of interaction, it aims to inspire researchers in both domains.

Research on materials containing transition metals that exhibit anomalous Hall effect is growing, although understanding this effect in triangular antiferromagnetic materials like Mn$_3$Sn requires further investigation. Our study explores how pressure influences the magnetic phase transitions in Mn$_3$Sn by combining experimental and computational methods. We find that high pressure training of Mn$_3$Sn samples reduces their magnetic susceptibility and demonstrates a room temperature anomalous Hall gap of approximately 0.06 eV, significantly lower than the zero-pressure gap of 0.06 eV. We attribute this gap to a non-zero Berry's curvature and verify that density functional theory calculations align with our experimental results. By simulating the effect of pressure on the material, we discovered that compressed Mn$_3$Sn exhibits increased magnetic ordering temperatures but decreased interlayer magnetic interactions. Our analysis also reveals that high pressure transforms the material from a metallic to a weakly semiconducting state, and we utilize the results from our zero-pressure analysis to explain the results obtained under pressure, finding that the anomalous Hall effect persists in the material even as it becomes semiconducting.

Formal knowledge acquisition from textual sources via the identification of relations between实体 is known as relation extraction (RE). This task has significant implications for semantic knowledge discovery and the development of knowledge bases. Over time, research in RE has seen a significant shift towards deep neural networks (DNNs), largely due to their superior performance in linking entities to their associated relations. This paper serves as a comprehensive guide to RE using DNNs, specifically focusing on the prominent patterns, concepts, architectural designs, training strategies, and evaluation techniques employed. A survey of 122 published studies is conducted, and the research is segmented into six primary areas: RE with prominent features in conjunction with various classifiers, RE utilizing deep models, hybrid approaches, semi-supervised learning methods, relation classification tasks guided by DNNs, and mention disambiguation. The paper concludes with an identification of promising research directions for the future development of RE using DNNs.

This study delves into a Steklov-Robin characteristic value problem within a limited,
bounded area in two dimensions. We establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions,
and demonstrate how they can be approximated by converting the problem into a monotone operator
issue and then applying the Picard iteration technique. The problem is further examined under
linear elasticity conditions, leading to the derivation of estimates for the values and an analysis
of the convergence rate in Lp spaces. The findings in this paper extend the existing knowledge
about Steklov and Robin problems.

The rapid advancement of video editing technologies depends heavily on robust frame restoration capabilities, especially when it comes to recovering hypergraphs that represent multiple viewpoints. Traditional approaches, like independent frame restoration, often neglect the inherent structural information, resulting in suboptimal outcomes. We introduce the guided hypergraph restoration method, which views each frame as a set of connected nodes and uses the inherent structure to enhance overall video quality. Our method's efficiency is evident in its ability to achieve high fidelity with a smaller number of output nodes, especially when compared to other models. In addition, our framework is versatile and can be easily integrated with other restoration models to yield superior results by leveraging the guided structure of hypergraphs.

This study presents an understanding of how chest X-rays are processed, 
resulting in the creation of the CXR CT Projection Dataset, which offers a 
comprehensive set of tasks and data features for training chest X-ray 
classification models. By using this new dataset, we examine the differences 
between reading chest X-rays and CT scans, and we demonstrate the 
limitations of current models trained on it. To overcome these issues, we 
developed projection models that directly train on projected images or closely 
mimic the processes radiologists employ to interpret 2D views from 3D scans. 
These enhanced models achieve superior performance on eight benchmark tests and 
produce more reliable predictions to assist radiologists. To further the 
research in this area, we propose a set of criteria to evaluate the 
reliability of chest X-ray models.

A contact form is designated as tight if it lacks a local or global Reeb ball property. Heegaard surface tightness implies the absence of tight Reeb flow lines, which in turn implies Euler characteristic constraints. Specifically, the handle decomposition of a tight contact form provides information about its Euler characteristic. The Thurston norm of a cohomology class can be expressed in terms of this Euler characteristic and a minimal-genus surface, which is determined by the attaching spheres of 2-handles in a Heegaard splitting. This norm has a lower bound in terms of the Euler characteristic and is shown to be achievable by certain min-gen surfaces. The problem of identifying transverse knots or transverse links that represent a given cohomology class and achieve the lower bound of the Thurston norm is formulated. The concept of a "thick" transverse knot is introduced, which indicates that the norm of the corresponding cohomology class achieves the lower bound. The Thurlston norm of the thick norm surface is shown to be equal to the lower bound of the Thurston norm and is found to be 0 for thick transverse knots in Genus(Σ) < 2, which contradicts a previously established theorem. Thick transverse knots in Genus(Σ) ≥ 2 may also exist and their thurston norm values may be non-zero. The contact boundary of thick transverse knots has specific geometric properties including geometric transverse genustoepstein and trans

We introduce a novel method for analyzing the flow of information within complex systems using entropic production rates. This method was specifically developed to evaluate the behavior of laser systems with complex microstructures. The entropic production rate in these lasers can be broken down into distinct contributions from different physical processes. In the case of microperforated laser media, one such contribution represents the average emission of photons from the system. The remaining contribution results from the interplay between light and matter within the artificial optical environment created by the microstructure. Notably, this rate can be positive, even in systems exhibiting overall irreversibility. This phenomenon occurs due to the organization of the photonic environment, which can sometimes result in a net decrease in entropy production as the system becomes more ordered. The magnitude of the 0 term, however, consistently reflects the dissipation of energy within the system and is always greater than the total entropic production rate.

The primary function of a cryptocurrency network, which incorporates mining and coins, is to serve as a self-sustaining and secure ledger for transaction records. The introduction of a cryptocurrency to an existing network necessitates adjusting the time interval for generating new blocks, which records transactions. When introducing a new cryptocurrency, selecting an appropriate time interval for block creation proves to be a challenging task. If the time interval is too short, the cost of mining becomes unnecessarily high. Conversely, if the time interval for mining is excessively long, the cryptocurrency network fails to record transactions swiftly enough, rendering it impractical for regular transactions. In this study, a formula is developed that considers the computational capabilities of miners and rewards for mining to establish a minimum time interval for mining, ensuring the maintenance of an intact cryptocurrency network. Furthermore, a model based on the Poisson distribution is employed to evaluate the maximum allowable time interval for mining and finding transactions. Numerical solutions are then presented for various parameters, demonstrating how the computational power of miners and mining rewards influence the permissible time interval for mining and finding transactions in a practical cryptocurrency network.

The widely-held belief that a system's long-term fluctuations approach a universal Airy distribution is challenged by an opposing viewpoint, with evidence suggesting recent experimental results and theoretical findings do not ultimately support this norm. What appears to be support for the fair noise theory often stems from an erroneous application of a framework used to determine probability distributions. We demonstrate that an analogous principle exists, but its correct implementation requires a specific correction. Implementation of this correction leads to various outcomes, either reaffirming the fair noise theory or providing probability distributions from which the theory can be derived. Although the theory has broad applicability beyond the KPZ equation, its fundamental tenets may not be accurate for all cases, with better descriptive terms possibly "faint noise" or "noisy decay."

Our analysis of MMS spacecraft data has provided the first evidence of compressive turbulence at sub-ion scales within the magnetic-field-parallel direction. Using both spacecraft observations and simulated data, we found that in both scenarios, the ratio of cross-spectral density to power spectral density varies differently based on frequency, with a distinct change in slope occurring at a specific frequency. The frequency at which this variation happens corresponds to the scale where anisotropy becomes significant. This finding enables the determination of the sub-ion scale anisotropic turbulence spectrum using data from individual spacecraft observations, a method we apply to a potential whistler wave event. The results show that the compressive fluctuation parallel to the magnetic field follows the $k_{\perp}^{-2.1}$ law at sub-ion scales for frequencies higher than the turnover frequency, which is consistent with previous research.

In the generation of XUV and soft X-ray free-electron laser (FEL) attosecond pulses, a conventional technique involves modulating electron bunches using a laser with a linearly increasing frequency. We present a novel approach based on the principle of chirp-tapering, as demonstrated experimentally at the Swiss Free-Electron Laser SESAME. Our algorithm automatically optimizes key parameters such as the optimal mean radius R_0 for various electron gun parameters and determines the optimal magnetic field profile B_0(R) for a given radius R_0. Our simulations show that the new method yields superior experiences per pulse and flash-to-flash stability when producing multimeV XUV and soft X-ray attosecond pulses.

The operator $\mathcal{O}$ is used to assess the operator $\mathcal{M}$, which predicts mean momentum in vertical shear flows with layered viscosity profiles. In a channel with a horizontal axis and vertical axis, these flows occur due to the influence of pressure in the horizontal axis and viscosity in the vertical axis. Using an expansion based on the ratio of the channel's vertical scale to its momentum viscosity, an initial prediction $\mathcal{M}$ is calculated and then corrected through numerical simulations to assess its accuracy in predicting effective viscosity. In low-viscosity areas, the predictions from the $\mathcal{O}$ operator were consistent with the numerical simulations. In viscosities that increase linearly, the $\mathcal{O}$ operator accurately predicted the corrected numerical simulations and matched tangential stress results from previous studies by M\"{u}nster and H\"{o}fmann. In viscosities that increase exponentially, the $\mathcal{O}$ operator accurately predicted the corrected numerical simulations but were significantly lower than the results from a related study by Schumacher and Sreenivasan. Schumacher and Sreenivasan had used direct numerical simulations to estimate the corrected values but found them difficult to accurately measure. In summary, the $\mathcal{O}$ operator provides a reliable method for predicting mean momentum in shear flows with varying viscosities, which can be used to study effective viscosity in geo-fluid dynamics.

The new evaluation metric is tested on real-world maps of United States states to demonstrate its practicality and effectiveness in assessing the fairness of various map configurations. The textile industry places significant emphasis on quality control to ensure high standards, particularly in patterned fabrics where defects are often subtle and can be overlooked by the human eye or standard inspection methods. To address this challenge, a novel technique combining the Guided Horizontal and Vertical Orientation (GHOG) feature descriptor with low-rank representation has been developed to efficiently identify flaws in patterned textile images. By leveraging the GHOG descriptor, which captures both texture and edge information, and leveraging the original image's low-rank nature, this new approach capitalizes on these characteristics to enhance defect detection accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that this technique outperforms the GOG and GHOG descriptors with the original descriptor's low-rank representation, ultimately showcasing its feasibility for practical application in modern textile factories.

We employ reinforcement learning to create an efficient and safe image
space planner for autonomous vehicle navigation. This planner uses data-
derived constraints to keep the generated trajectories on a path with high
sensing confidence, thus avoiding complex and hazardous environments. In
addition, we exploit the capability of deep reinforcement learning planners
to adapt to unknown or dynamic environments by using data-driven constraints
that reflect the current environment's exploration pattern. This adaptive
policy learning approach, named adaptive data-driven reinforcement learning
policy, demonstrates superior performance and safety in simulation and real
world driving tests when compared to traditional model-predictive control
methods.

As a black hole absorbs matter and grows, the intensity of its gravitational wave emission peaks when its radius is about three times the Schwarzschild radius, causing it to experience "ringing" and temporarily slowing down its mass loss. This phenomenon, however, leads to the formation of an information paradox, where the black hole appears to violate unitarity in quantum mechanics. An attempt to resolve this issue, where gravity remains weak, is made by calculating the entropy of external gravitational fields, which must exceed the black hole's entropy to avoid creating a high-entropy black hole from matter with more degrees of freedom than gravity has microstates. This solution, however, has challenges, where our understanding of long-range gravitational fields is limited, making the theoretical approach less convincing. This letter aims to explore an alternative approach to solving the issue, where we derive a mass-reduction rate limit by considering the instability of hypothetical "hair" on the black hole's surface due to rotational effects, where we model the gravitational field as a scalar field and analyze its behavior under angular instability. This leads to the establishment of a mass-reduction rate, where we consider various scenarios and find that our result aligns with predictions from holographic models and scalar-tensor theories, ultimately yielding a specific formula for the mass-reduction rate.

Deep within dense environments like the galactic center, the first stars die and leave behind a trail of objects that continue to collide under the influence of gravity. These collisions generate ripples in space-time that can be detected by future telescopes. To understand better what these collisions might look like, scientists conducted simulations to study how objects orbiting each other in galactic nuclei behave. They found that while most black holes form through these interactions and can potentially generate significant ripples in space-time, a small number of objects are left over and can also engage in destructive battles under the influence of gravity, especially when they settle into a lower orbit. These leftover objects have a higher chance of generating detectable ripples in space-time compared to the wider population. To increase the likelihood of discovering these waves in space-time, researchers recommend searching for signs of objects orbiting lower than a certain threshold.

To address data availability issues in advanced power distribution system operations, event-based power distribution systems need precise timing information for forecasting error rates and developing decision support tools. With the growing integration of renewable energy sources and smart loads, power distribution networks will generate vast amounts of data that can be utilized for data-driven event-based power distribution systems. This research proposes an innovative approach to identify key occurrences in power distribution systems by analyzing data from sensors and meters installed on transformers, circuits, buses, feeders, and other components. This event-driven data will provide crucial information for system operators to update models and refine existing algorithms. With the growing deployment of phasor measurement units, phasor estimation, and communication technology, the accuracy and reliability of time-stamped event data will significantly improve. This concept paper outlines a framework for identifying events within power distribution networks, the challenges associated with event identification, and potential solutions involving machine learning and deep learning techniques.

Within  effective hadronic interaction  chiral perturbation theory, we investigate transitions of the enigmatic $X(3872)$ across hadronic channels by applying both approaches, but with limited success only for the $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ process. Notably, our differential decay rate results for this process show substantial disagreement with measured data, and we discuss possible ways to mitigate this disparity. Furthermore, our theoretical framework is found unsuitable for describing the $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \epsilon$ channel.

We define specific categories associated with quadratic forms over fields, establishing relationships between these categories and identifying invariants of the quadratic forms based on category morphisms. It is decided which quadratic forms have a non-trivial endomorphism ring, and the minimal invariant identified. Furthermore, for the purpose of comparison, we developed categories over symmetric bilinear forms and identified their relationship with the quadratic form categories, confirming that they yield the same category. Consequently, we concluded that any characteristic of a quadratic form over a field of characteristic 2 is also a characteristic of any quadratic form over its quadratic closure.

Text-based games provide a text interface for playing, offering an accessible platform to simulate these games and interact with players via the interface.  Emulating text-based games is beneficial as it allows the playing of older games without the need for the original software and supports the development of text-based games for players who are visually impaired.  However, text-based game emulation can be challenging due to the large number of actions required to play a game, requiring the emulator to handle up to 100,000 individual actions per move, a significant computational burden.  Effective game play also necessitates finding efficient action sequences with minimal length while avoiding invalid actions or getting stuck in loops.  The problem is further complicated by the need for the emulator to execute thousands of environment interactions in a short period of time, particularly when using reinforcement learning algorithms that require multiple iterations.  The computational demands are exemplified by the 55 million turns necessary for solutions found by recent reinforcement learning approaches in one of the games of the textworld benchmark.  To address these challenges, this study proposes a highly efficient near-optimal tree access action queueing system that facilitates rapid emulation of text-based games, executing as many as 160,000 actions per millisecond, and demonstrates significant improvements over existing solutions by reducing the required environmental interactions by a factor of 1000 foradventitious solutions or up to a factor of 10,000 for near-optimal strategies.

To adapt topological insulator theories that assume perfect geometric flaws to cases where pentagons, heptagons, and other irregular polygons are involved, we developed a new technique. Using this approach, we were able to apply the bulk boundary correspondence and establish a clear link between the bulk invariant and the boundary state, even in cases where traditional methods fail. Our results show that the key relationship between the Chern number and the Berry curvature remains valid, regardless of the type of defect present, and this was verified through both theoretical reasoning and numerical simulations of the hexagonal model.

Hadamard's formula for the absolute value of a $p$-harmonic function within a half-plane is recalled and multiple extensions of this formula are presented for $p$-harmonic functions in various two-dimensional sectors. These examples also lead to the formula's application in proving inequalities for $p$-harmonic functions in specific sectors or on certain $p$-harmonic curves.

The study applies a multivariate extreme value approach to model extreme ocean environments using data from a Typhoon forrest forecast model. Employing a typhoon-conditional method, the research incorporates the effect of a storm's intensity and path on a forecast grid. The analysis utilizes a case study of Typhoon Durong in 1994 to demonstrate the application of the method in extreme sea level modeling under different ocean boundary conditions. The study highlights the significance of the research in supporting marine operations and environmental policy-making through the estimation of extreme values in specific ocean regions during a storm.

Let K be a number field and let's consider two polynomials, $f$ and $g$, with coefficients in the ring of integers of K. We are looking at the composite functions $f^n$ and $g^n$. Our research demonstrates that there are only a finite number of non-constant functions that can be raised to various powers and still result in a pair of functions that never coincide over the course of all natural number exponents n.

A recently developed method seeks to enhance a humanoid robot's ability to perform manipulation tasks with a planned motion trajectory and a human companion guiding them through physical cues. An approach utilizing an iterative iteration was proposed to synchronize the human and robot movements while maintaining a constant distance between them for a smooth transfer experience. Despite showing promising results, this method faced challenges due to inaccuracies in estimating human position, leading to disruptions in their interaction. Our study aims to resolve this limitation through the creation of an on-manifold adjustment technique based on the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm. This new technique estimates the human's position with a higher degree of accuracy while preserving their relative orientation, ensuring a seamless transfer experience. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this new technique in a real-world setting with a 7DOF Series II Exoskeleton and a 7DOT Atlas Robot.

The matrix element technique has been used to investigate Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{H}\textrm{H}\textrm{ \to } \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC with a 13 TeV proton-proton collision energy. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the matrix element technique in enhancing signal sensitivity and reducing background interference. Specifically, it exhibits a 10-20% increase in signal and a 10-30% decrease in background depending on the cut values, ultimately yielding an approximately 20% improvement in the overall performance of the analysis.

Our goal is to develop a method that enables robots to comprehend their environment in a 3D coordinate system. Currently, supervisory learning of 3D coordinates is a challenging task.  Robots can acquire coordinate understanding by utilizing entropic value regularized exploration (EERe) to learn a policy that maximizes 3D distinct views discovered.  We demonstrate that robots can learn coordinate perception through intentional and unintentional rotations while exploring, focusing on learning rotation axes and directions as part of the process. In our experiments, robots learned these characteristics by observing objects rotating intentionally and unintentionally. Furthermore, we show that acquired rotation skills enhance other capabilities including shape reconstruction and 3D object localization.

This research addresses the challenge of distinguishing between social media users who accept or reject COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation and aims to fill a knowledge gap by filling it with a new dataset and task for multi-turn conversation. The proposed task and dataset involve leveraging context and user profiles in social media to determine whether individuals accept or reject misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines. This work also introduces a new NLI-based methodology and methodology for evaluating model performance in this area. Empirical results from experiments demonstrate that our proposed methodology is effective and that future improvements can potentially be achieved by incorporating more nuanced feature engineering techniques.

To explore the dynamics of isolated attosecond pulse generation, we conducted full quantum mechanical simulations using a strong and uniform electric field in the vacuum. A two-cycle strong field pulse successfully produced an isolated attosecond burst of extreme UV radiation by facilitating a symmetric and balanced process of tunnel ionization, photon emission, and recombination. Our simulations revealed that minor disturbances in the strong field, such as those arising from ripplons at the vacuum plasma boundary, still enable the creation of isolated attosecond pulses. Moreover, precise control over these pulses, including their emission time, emission probability, and final kinetic energy, can be achieved by adjusting the amplitude and phase of the applied field. Our study provides a starting point for designing isolated attosecond pulse trains governed by strong, stable fields to investigate electron dynamics.

Recent discoveries of companions in single-line eclipsing binary systems often signal the presence of tertiary bodies. A comprehensive search for these elusive tertiary companions in Algol systems is missing from the literature. A research team analyzed 336 such systems in the vicinity of the Galactic plane, obtaining light curves spanning 10 to 25 years from the Wide Field B Survey. A meticulous examination of the light curve segments yielded 35 tertiary detections, corresponding to a comprehensive detection rate of approximately 10%. Notably, the detection rate was observed to be notably higher for systems with shorter periods. To put the research results into perspective, the team compared their findings with existing simulations and conclusions drawn from radial velocity studies. The study confirms the widespread presence of companions in Algol systems and provides valuable insights into the formation and evolution of these complex celestial systems.

This research focuses on determining the minimum strength of a potential, denoted as $V_0$, required to cause instant explosion in the $L^2$-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation outside a convex barrier. We discovered that this minimum strength lies within the range of scaled potentials of the optimal focusing quadratic potential. Numerical tests confirm that potential parameters at one extreme of our results are achievable.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) by integrating physical knowledge into a machine learning framework that can solve both discretized and continuous problems without necessitating mesh generation. Although PINNs circumvent many traditional numerical challenges, they introduce a novel one: how to effectively balance computational resources to achieve the desired solution accuracy. We introduce Residual-Driven Adaptive Node Creation (RANG), a novel node-based refinement strategy for PINNs that dynamically creates new computational nodes in areas with high solution complexity. By replacing existing physical knowledge representations with multilevel feedforward neural networks at these nodes, RANG concentrates computational resources where they are most needed. We evaluate RANG's performance in solving two benchmark problems and compare it to other adaptive PINNs techniques, demonstrating that our method efficiently balances the trade-off between solution accuracy and computational cost.

The combination of negative capacitance (NC) devices and domain walls has the potential to improve energy efficiency in modern electronics. A novel FET structure featuring a ferroelectric domain wall offers a solution to control channel conductivity at the atomic level. This paper explores the properties of multi-domain FeFETs through the use of a comprehensive simulator that incorporates complex dynamics within the device. By examining the behavior of these transistors, we have uncovered the existence of an over-shooting phenomenon during turn-off. This has the potential to be leveraged for creating ultra-low power, multi-bit storage integrated circuits. Additionally, our simulations have been validated by experimental data on a 32nm FeFET technology platform.

This study deploys a structural model called the freight ecosystem dependency-fragility insight graph (FSIG) to map the intricate relationships between various sectors of the freight transportation system and the effects of disruptions to those sectors. The FSIG framework is founded on the concept of ecosystem dependency-fragility analysis, which is used to evaluate the stability of economic systems in the presence of disruptions to their constituent parts. The FSIG methodology combines aspects of network science and game theory to create a comprehensive visual representation of freight transportation interdependencies and potential cascading effects of disruptions to various parts of the system. The framework was applied to the United States freight transportation system to offer a general overview of the potential impacts of disruptions to its various sectors. The analysis identified regions that are most susceptible to disruption spread within the US freight transportation system during different types of disruptions. Additionally, the research finds that certain US regions tend to experience more significant disruptions in their local economies when there is a disruption originating in a different region, which provides valuable insights for understanding the potential effects of disruptions in the freight transportation system.

This study delves into the ergodic properties of an intricate Ginzburg-Landau equation subject to stochastic perturbations via a Poisson measure and multiplicative noise. The researchers to consider stochastic disturbances as pure jump disturbances generated by a independent infinitesimal generator multiplicative C$_{0}$-semigroup. The theory of stochastic partial differential equations is employed, enabling the researchers to establish sufficient conditions for ensuring strong Feller property and irreducibility for the stochastic system. The researchers further demonstrate the existence of a stationary, ergodic measure for the stochastic system as a direct application of their main results. The resulting theoretical findings have broad implications in physics, physics in engineering, and the theoretical study of stochastic dynamical systems.

Let G be a finite group and denote by $\mathcal{L}(G)$ the maximum value of the minimal degrees of non-linear irreducible complex characters for all nilpotent groups containing a given subgroup G, in normalization by the order of G to the power of a specific exponent. This maximum value is attained when G is the direct product of its Sylow p-subgroups for various prime numbers p, in which case $\mathcal{L}(G)$ is the maximum character degree for its p-component $G_p$, in notation $\mathcal{L}(G) = \max_{p}\mathcal{L}(G_p)$. For abelian groups specifically, this maximum value is determined for all prime numbers p and is also the maximum achievable value.

A cutting-edge Hadron Spectrometer has been meticulously designed to study the properties of hadrons in detailed ways. The instrument is specifically tailored for the LHC and is intended to provide highly accurate measurements of the longitudinal momentum of neutral and charged hadrons. By doing so, the Spectrometer will be able to identify the sources of these particles, including whether they come from the interaction point of the LHC, the atmosphere, or cosmic sources.
