Its sophisticated design incorporates specialized detectors for particles with charges and energy levels, as well as a highly precise timing system to locate the interaction point at the LHC with great accuracy. By gathering a vast amount of data on the movement of these particles over time, the Spectrometer will be able to create comprehensive diagrams of the changes in the movement of such particles and their partners and fill in significant gaps in current knowledge. By detecting rare events, the Spectrometer will be able to study the stability of the LHC and other key points and enhance our understanding of the stability of the LHC. By doing so, the Spectrometer will be able to significantly advance the field of nuclear physics. By setting extremely low limits on the stability of the LHC and other key points, the Spectrometer will be able to enhance our understanding of the stability of the LHC. By doing so, the Spectrometer will be able to significantly advance the field of nuclear physics.

The primary goal of image identification is image classification, but it also encompasses image recognition, which includes determining the category and possible orientation of an image. Since most existing deep neural networks are not designed to handle image rotation, we introduce a novel convolutional architecture that recognizes both the orientation and category of an image. By introducing orientation-sensitive filters, our network can learn features that change based on the image's orientation, allowing it to accurately identify the orientation and category. Our results on the CIFAR-100 dataset demonstrate that our network achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in image rotation-based classification tasks.

Geometric data processing using Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) on point cloud inputs has gained attention in the deep learning community. Notably, GCNs have shown success in tasks such as 3D semantic segmentation and part segmentation. However, these tasks often involve sparse and unstructured point cloud data, which poses a challenge for GCN implementation. In this study, a novel GCN setup is proposed for GCN-based tasks on point cloud data. Our main findings address three key questions: the influence of node feature overfitting, the importance of connecting layers to handle sparse data, and the efficacy of pre-existing public datasets. Through experiments on various datasets, the proposed setup demonstrates superior performance in 3D semantic and part segmentation tasks. The proposed method and code are available at https://github.com/3DV-CV/3D-CV-GCN-Setup.

Research into Neural Network integrity has been a primary concern. The beneficial effects of adversarial examples have positive implications, yet their potential vulnerabilities pose a significant threat. The research challenge lies in uncovering adversarial examples that convey no clear meaning. Although existing studies focus on creating adversarial samples, they fail to delve into the process by which adversarial samples are created. To this end, this investigation aims to develop a new hostless Trojan attack - Semantic Adversarial Example Generation (SAEG), using a Universal Adversarial Trigger Network (UATN). Unlike previous research, SAEG employs a network trained on training data, incorporating adversarial samples with distinct patterns. This enables any model with its corresponding trigger to detect and identify adversarial samples across any model, regardless of the training set. The proposed method uses the network's knowledge accumulated during training to create distinct patterns recognizable by any model with its specific trigger. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of SAEG in generating meaningful Trojan samples, while also demonstrating the feasibility of detecting adversarial samples using only the pattern learned during training. Furthermore, this investigation examines the computational complexity of UATN and compares its back propagation process with the original training data process.

We present an update on the ROSIE Integral Field Unit development on the Magellan IMACS IMACS spectrometer, where we introduce an updated installation at the Coudé focal plane with enhanced design features. The current setup has been upgraded with a new imaging system with higher spatial resolution, a broader wavelength detection range of 400-1700 Angstroms and significantly improved signal efficiency. The cross-dispersion resolution has been increased to 0.33 arcseconds compared to the previous 0.50 arcseconds. Additionally, our cross-dispersion resolution exhibits minimal variation with wavelength. The RosIE team continues to utilize the upgraded IFU for scientific data collection and 5 years of public data are accessible on the APASS website.

This paper delves into the research of carbon-12 to carbon-12 nuclear collisions, examining key aspects such as the Coulomb barrier height, fusion cross-sections, and coupling effects, with a focus on understanding their significance in nuclear physics. Additionally, the article explores the adaptation of the Trojan horse technique for enhancing the measurement accuracy of fusion cross-sections at lower energy ranges and determining the nuclear interaction range.

The vast number of exoplanets discovered so far exceeds our current understanding of terrestrial planet formation. To bridge this understanding gap, researchers explored how planetary mass influences water and volatiles incorporation. A key factor here is planetary composition, particularly the core's chemical makeup. By examining observed stars around planets, they analyzed water and alkali metals in their photospheres, allowing them to infer the planetary core's composition. Their study shows that planetary mass and core mass are linearly correlated, demonstrating that mass a particular way affects cores a certain way. As a result, they found that the amount of water in Earth-mass planets depends on the amount of core metals in their母星, whereas massive planets likely incorporate more water and suppress their母星 alkali elements. Their findings align with the magma ocean model, particularly for massive planets, and suggest that water and alkali metals were suppressed during their母星 accretion.

The capabilities of WiFi signals penetrate obstacles at the chip scale, enabling them to gather substantial spatial information. Conventionally used for data transmission, WiFi can be leveraged to perform precise positioning. The complexity of the resulting channel state information (CSI) hinders the extraction of relevant information under conventional approaches. In this study, we limit the consideration to the vertical penetration of WiFi signals, leading to the identification of periodic patterns within the channel responses. Consequently, we limit the useful CSI features to these patterns and utilize a 1D CNN to classify the penetration depth of targets based on these features. Furthermore, we develop an attention mechanism to emphasize the critical channel observations for the estimation of distance. The proposed method has been validated using a custom data collection set comprising nearly 200 labels in a controlled setting, yielding a 50cm average error reduction compared to current solutions. Additionally, our method demonstrates robust performance across diverse environments due to its reliance on the underlying CSI characteristics, exhibiting minimal performance degradation in real-world scenarios due to minimal irrelevant noise incorporation.

This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for the semantic interpretation of basic modal logic with the N operator, where the logical system (B) is expanded to incorporate the Markov rule (MB). In this context, the Markov rule signifies that if a proposition is true at any point in time, it was also true in the past. This paper defines the logical system (B) as (Lob) integrated with (N), and systematically explores various modal correspondences within the framework. A key contribution of this research is the establishment of a topological interpretation where the topological space components are closed, and the modal correspondence relations serve as open sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both the topological and set-theoretic interpretations of (B) integrate the logical system (Lob) and the local truth system (T), respectively. An important finding of this research is the topological distinction between the logical systems (Lob) and (T), which were previously shown to be distinguishable through the set-theoretic interpretation of these systems. Ultimately, this paper proves the completeness of the basic modal logic with the N operator relative to the proposed topological interpretation.

A bipartite graph's edges can be colored individually, while a face is defined by a sequence of edges that aren't adjacent. The modified 4-edge coloring problem involves bipartite graphs where the maximum number of colors used is minimized, resulting in a coloring where every color class consists solely of edges. A recent paper claimed to solve the modified 4-edge coloring problem for bipartite graphs with specific constraints: they needed to have at least $4n-10$ edges. However, this claim is incorrect, and an example of a bipartite graph with the required number of edges that can't be properly colored was submitted to the article.

This research explores the Hamming distance within an n-dimensional binary space,
denoted as H(n), and its corresponding Fourier transform, with the aim of determining a lower bound for
the minimum support of a function f, where f is constrained by a specific set of constraints
imposed upon the Hamming distance. To achieve this goal, we first investigate the properties
of the Hamming distance, its linear span, and the associated Fourier transform. H(n)'s
distance characteristics are found to be solely dependent on its degree set, leading to a
function with a minimum support of k + 2 when the degree satisfies certain conditions related to the
conflict with k. By extending this finding, we derive a general expression for the minimum
support of functions with a specified degree, utilizing both the nonvanishing property and
the conflict concept. A lower bound of n/2 is established for the minimum support, where the
half-conflict idea is also introduced in this study. Ultimately, the method employed to resolve
the minimum support problem involves identifying the minimum support cardinality for functions
that vanish outside a specified subspace of H(n).

COPASI, a simulation tool with wide usage, enables users to build and analyze complex models across areas like biochemistry and network science. Its capabilities for data fit and advanced data analysis are highly advanced. Nevertheless, setting up and interpreting these models can be complicated due to its interface. We introduced ShinyCOPASI, a simplified, web-based interface that allows users to easily utilize COPASI's capabilities, featuring an integrated library of pre-made networks and customizable options for investigators.

Deep learning methods have become widely used in the fields of computer vision and image processing, largely due to their ability to provide simple and effective solutions for complex tasks. However, these methods still face significant challenges in achieving high precision, reliability, and interpretability. Although deep learning methods have demonstrated strong capabilities in the diagnosis of skin cancer, their reliability remains unverified in high-stakes clinical settings. This study introduces a new framework for measuring and evaluating the reliability of deep learning methods in the context of high-stakes clinical applications, with a particular focus on skin cancer diagnosis. The proposed framework encompasses novel concepts and evaluation techniques, including the introduction of virtual pathologists as a reliable gold-standard reference, and a comprehensive analysis of model uncertainties. The study proposes a systematic approach for assessing the reliability of deep learning methods, including a novel evaluation protocol that considers user uncertainties in clinical settings. In addition, the study proposes a set of principles and standards for machine intelligence applications in medical settings, including the evaluation of reliability before other metrics such as accuracy and accuracy rate. The proposed framework and principles provide a foundation for the development and evaluation of more reliable and interpretable machine intelligence methods in medical settings.

Let's denote $\mathcal{K}$ as the von Neumann algebra of all category functions on a compact quantum group $\alpha:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}^\ast$. The paper establishes conditions under which $\mathcal{K}$ possesses specific properties. The study focuses particularly on the quantum permutation group $S_n^\ast$ and determines the dimension of $\mathcal{K}$ for $S_n^\ast$.

This study proposes a novel strategy iteration strategy that can deal with uncertainty in Q-matrix formulations of Markov decision processes (MDPs). By introducing both lower and upper value iterates along with corresponding policy evaluations, this approach generates two converging sequences that bound the optimal value function. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through numerical experiments that show it is capable of converging to an accurate approximation of the optimal value function even with limited precision. In contrast to strategy iteration, which can become trapped in local optima and may fail to converge under certain conditions, this method always achieves convergence.

In a significant result from Herzog, Popescu, and Vladoiu, a formula for the core of monomial ideals in polynomial rings was provided. Building on this result, we first derived the core of monomial ideals with two generators that share a common monomial. Subsequently, applying these findings to the edge ideals of weighted directed graphs, we identified the Grobner basis with respect to a specific term order for the edge ideal of a weighted directed graph, given that its underlying undirected graph is a forest. This allowed us to compute the core of these ideals, which in turn enabled the calculation of the parameter $\nu_I$ for such ideals, which represent invariants of the associated numerical semigroups. Furthermore, we investigated the term order Grobner deformation of the edge ideals of certain directed paths and determined the core of such ideals.

This paper investigates an inverse problem associated with time-series data generated by computer simulations of complex systems. We analyze a one-dimensional Ising model under specific conditions for parameter T, observing how the distribution of T impacts model outputs. Our goal is to identify values of T for which simulations align with empirical data, obtained from real-world measurements. We employ multi-objective optimization techniques to investigate the data. Our research contributes to the field by applying these optimizations to computer models, providing insights into the behavior of complex systems and informing forward simulations.

This study investigates Resistant Learning using a scenario-based learning framework where multiple agents learn a game on a grid with hidden objectives. The game's complexity increases with grid size, and hidden objectives are represented as regional queries. These queries help an agent learn its local environment while avoiding areas where other agents are learning, thereby preventing query contamination that could stall learning progress. Regional queries ensure that each agent's learning progress can be verified by the existence of a winning path query. We use various grid sizes to evaluate the effectiveness of a query strategy and measure the differences in learning efficiency between non-regional and regional query approaches. Our findings indicate that the cost of generating regional queries is negligible compared to the benefits they provide, especially as grid sizes grow.

The reconstruction of isolated-photon-tagged jets in Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV, within a specific transverse momentum range and centrality range, reveals significant changes in charged-particle associated-hadron distributions relative to proton-proton collisions. This deviation is characterized by reduced associated-hadron density and increased forward-pepting, indicating the influence of QCD interactions and medium effects on jet fragmentation. By comparing hadron-spheron correlations with specific momentum ratios, we infer that CHADron correlations are more impacted by radiative processes than elastic collisions. These findings suggest that CHADron correlations may be a valuable tool for assessing energy loss mechanisms in the quark-gluon plasma.

Recent research involving hypergeometric series with parameters and multiple zeta values has been the focus of multiple studies, including those by the current authors. Building on previous findings, this paper reveals that certain non-alternating series can be expressed through combinations of colored multiple zeta values. As an example, the Papperozzer identity has been expressed in the following form:

$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(1/2)_{n}^{3}}{(3/2)_{n}^{3}} z^{n} = F_{{{\begin{array}{c}
1,1,1\\
1,1,1
\end{array}}}}(z) + F_{{{\begin{array}{c}
1\\
1,1,1
\end{array}}}}(z) + F_{{{\begin{array}{c}
1,1\\
1,1
\end{array}}}}(z) + F_{{{\begin{array}{c}
1\\
1
\end{array}}}}(z),$

where $F$ represents specific polylogarithmic series. Utilizing this identity, the authors derive a novel hypergeometric approximation that shares similarities with the Apéry series, which played a pivotal role in proving the irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$.

A brown dwarf located approximately 47.5 parsecs away, with a mass similar to that of Jupiter, has an unusual story behind its discovery and characterization. The object, first observed in a photometric survey of brown dwarfs, was then studied in detail through spectroscopy, revealing highly unexpected findings that contradict standard models. The brown dwarf has extremely low metallicity and exhibits extremely broad spectral features, similar to those of the exoplanet ROAPAS-39, discovered through radial velocity searches. The two objects share several striking similarities in their compositions and evolutionary histories, suggesting a potential common origin related to formation within metal-poor galaxies. Understanding the unusual brown dwarf's properties may provide important insights into the complex processes of galaxy and planetary formation.

Our study investigates the production, suppression patterns and yield ratios of various particles created in mid-rapidity regions of 21.6 GeV $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ Xe-Xe collisions on a per pair basis. These evaluation criteria include the production of certain types of quark combinations in these collisions. Initial data collection involved 2.13 million charged particles tracked in a central 25% rapidity range using the T0, D0 and WVP detectors of the STAR experiment. Results reveal a significant increase in the production of these particles as the collision energy rises from a lower energy of 2.76 TeV in PeVPeV collisions to a higher energy of 5.44 TeV in NaVNaV collisions. Further analysis also shows varying suppression patterns of these particles as the density of the collisions changes. Additionally, findings also indicate lower production of certain types of quark combinations in NaVNaV collisions compared to other types of collisions at the same energy level.

We have developed a novel, straightforward approach to interpolate parton distribution functions (PDFs) within the Bjorken-x range where data is scarce, and a straightforward method to progress PDFs to higher Q^2 values using the lowest available Q^2 value as a reference. Our approach simplifies the commonly employed Lorentzian parameterization to basic exponential forms, and builds upon DGLAP code solutions by employing them directly. We have integrated a straightforward multiplicative function into the x-dependent PDF at a lower scale, and evaluated the impact of this addition using the OMM scheme at the lowest Q^2 value. Our approach was tested using the CT10 QCD PDF set at Q^2 = 100 GeV to predict PDFs at higher Q^2 values (1000 GeV) in the Bjorken-x range where data is lacking. These predictions were compared to the original CT10 PDFs, showing only minor deviations. Using the predicted PDFs to calculate standard model particle cross-sections yielded no significant differences when contrasted with the original CT10 results.

In-situ construction on other celestial bodies like the Moon and Mars is a key goal for future expeditions and long-term colonization. Utilizing local regolith for constructing habitats and habitation could bypass the need to transport expansive amounts of conventional building materials from Earth. Regolith's high melting point and contaminants make it challenging to use and studies have shown that heat treatment improves its bindability through unknown microstructural and mechanical processes. This study aims to investigate the bindability and mechanical properties of heat-treated Martian, Lunar soil and Chondrules through compression, microscopy, and spectroscopy to better understand the binding mechanism.

The impact of shear on the Rayleigh-Plateau instability in a hanging liquid film was investigated. 
For a film on a non-moving support, the effect of shear was found to be minimal. 
Conversely, when the film is on a moving cylinder, the wind-induced shear significantly alters the critical wavelength of the undulations. 
Our analytical results show that at low wind speeds, where surface shear stress is much less than gravity times the film thickness, the critical wavelength is well understood and relates to the undetermined parameter in the problem. 
By numerically solving the relevant equations, we identified the regime boundaries in a diagram that helps select the appropriate theoretical approach. 
Comparison with previous experimental and numerical studies confirms the accuracy of our findings.

Recent observations from the WLTH survey have enabled the derivation of star formation rates for several low-mass star clusters. By comparing the $H\alpha$ derived star formation rates from SED fittings with the $B$-$\gamma$ relationship, we can assess the accuracy of star formation rate measurements. Our analysis shows that the $B$-$\gamma$ relationship generally aligns with the more established diagnostic methods and generally agrees within a factor of 2-3 in most cases, though some discrepancies may arise. Several factors may be responsible for these discrepancies and their magnitude. Moreover, by taking into account additional constraints, such as dust masses, we can further refine our estimates of star formation rates. Ultimately, the large scatter in $B$-$\gamma$ derived star formation rates may be attributed to variations in stellar population models, which may affect rate of low-mass star formation across different star clusters.

This paper delves into the B-type quantum subalgebra of $\mathfrak{sl}_{2r}$, specifically denoted as $qo(2r+1)$. It defines a bivariate quantum invariant, and investigates its impact on the highest weight key modules. Crucially, it derives an explicit formula for the finite-dimensional subalgebra of $u_q(\mathfrak{sl}_{2r})$, which is denoted as $U_q(\Lambda)$. This subalgebra has a significant effect on the key module of $qo(2r+1)$. It's also demonstrated that $U_q(\Lambda)$ is equivalent to the Type B quantum subalgebra of $u_q(\mathfrak{sl}_N)$.

The concept of EMD has emerged as a prominent solution for various unsupervised and semi-supervised learning tasks. Despite this, researchers have difficulty in finding a suitable diffusion process for EMD. We initially demonstrate that enforcing marginal constraints on traditional diffusion processes leads to a lack of convergence in many real-world applications. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that ensures marginal constraints are met even at early stages of the diffusion process. This approach will inevitably compromise the optimality solution of EMD. As a result, we derive clear and easily computable conditions for determining the minimum variance of the diffusion process. Upon examining various existing diffusion models, we discover that only the Gaussian distribution satisfies the derived conditions. Ultimately, we present a theoretical proof that shows the optimality of our solution for the EMD universal diffusion problem.

In recent years, the interest in identifying handwritten mathematical expressions has gained prominence due to advances in interactive learning technologies. While there is extensive research on reading single characters and words by hand, the equivalent for capturing and recognizing complex expressions in their continuous form is relatively new. To bridge this gap, we have developed and introduced a new dataset that captures handwritten expressions in their continuous form using a graphical tablet integrated with a graphical interface. This interface enables a seamless connection between sensor data and the written characters. Moreover, we have outlined and experimentally verified a novel framework for analyzing this unique modal input and transforming it into a reading task, ultimately facilitating hand-written mathematical expression recognition. Our results show that the proposed approach yields competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods.

The goal of the speech duration assignment task is to determine the start and end times of phonemes based on their length, which in turn relies on calculating the duration of each. While many approaches exist, many are heavily dependent on the accuracy of actual speech duration samples, which can be severely limited by privacy restrictions and copyright. To address this limitation, we introduce a median-of-environment length creation technique that utilizes a non-statistic length creation method, which divides speech into segments at each phoneme and splits them into two groups based on their relative length compared to the median, eliminating the need for real speech samples. To assess the effectiveness of this method, we apply it to the speech duration of the fundamental frequency, which serves as an indicator of speech quality, and compare the results with the speech length derived from the actual vocal frequency. The results show that the proposed non-statistic method yields a average absolute difference of 118.11ms (73.14%) from the speech length derived from the actual vocal frequency, demonstrating its feasibility for speech duration assignment even in the absence of real speech samples.

Conservation planning through species distribution modeling is crucial, requiring integration of species' occurrence probabilities with habitat suitability assessments. Integrated analysis of these factors helps optimize resource allocation and understanding of species interactions. However, current approaches often fail to account for spatial autocorrelation and collinearity in data, which can compromise model validity and compromise conservation measures. Introducing the spHabitat package, a specialized tool addressing these issues in both single and multi-species models, along with a Bayesian hierarchical approach to handling spatial and ecological processes. Introducing the spHabitat package, a specialized tool addressing these issues in both single and multi-species models, along with a Bayesian hierarchical approach to handling both the spatial and ecological processes.

Skin cancer is the most prevalent form of cancer in the US and accounts for over 500,000 new cases each year. While dermatologists have the ultimate decision-making power in diagnosing and treating skin lesions, the final decision is often influenced by digital imaging tools such as dermoscopy. Traditional computer-aided diagnosis systems focus on quantifying cancer-related features in digital images in an effort to enhance diagnostic accuracy. However, these systems have been criticized for lacking the depth of interaction with complex clinical features. The Skincare initiative aims to overcome these limitations by developing an innovative, highly interactive machine learning framework for the automatic diagnosis of skin lesions from digital images. The framework's strength lies in its highly adaptable architecture, which can be easily modified to accommodate various clinical objectives and interact with users in a multitude of ways. The Skincare initiative's initial contribution is the presentation of the SkinDeep, a cutting-edge interactive machine learning system for the diagnosis of skin cancers from dermoscopic images. The framework leverages profound learning techniques and adapts them to the challenges associated with the diagnosis of skin cancers. It also presents the SkinDeep's comprehensive evaluation and compares its outcomes with the current state-of-the-art methods in the field. The SkinDeep's ultimate goal is to assist dermatologists in their cancer diagnosis process.

To enhance the accuracy of cosmological redshift determinations for Type Ia supernovae, our research suggests the use of a Stochastic Autoencoder incorporating a Latent Variable with Gaussian distribution derived from high-quality, multi-epoch SN Ia spectra data. By applying this approach, our results indicate that our model's capability in classifying SN Ia spectra surpasses established techniques in the literature. Furthermore, our findings also highlight the potential for improved distance modulus-redshift relations using our stochastical approach.

High-resolution near-infrared integral field spectroscopy has been obtained for a strongly lensed star-forming galaxy at an expansion rate of 2.21 and apparent size of 1.66 kiloparsecs by using the Extremely Large Telescope. This study reveals a massive star formation activity within the galaxy, centered on low-efficiency gas dynamics as suggested by an elevated 3-4 disk-specific energy. We identify distinct near-infrared emission lines and map their spatial distribution across the galaxy, discovering glowing filaments up to 3 kiloparsecs long, likely representing neutral outflows moving at speeds of 85 kilometers per second and emitting carbon and oxygen-rich photons. We model the dynamics and emission of these filaments, estimating a low disk-specific energy consistent with outflow-driven neutrals at sub-parsec scales. We conclude that a galaxy-wide neutrational outflow propagates throughout the galaxy, triggering and channeling star formation within it, rather than issuing from multiple separate star-forming regions within it. This study highlights a relationship between a galaxy's properties and its behavior, emphasizing disk-specific energy as a marker for neutral gas dynamics at low densities as well as for the study of gravity-driven and neutrational outflows within it.

The growth dynamics of turbulent plumes are significantly altered in the presence of suspended particles by the drag they impose. This effect becomes particularly noticeable when the ratio of particle to fluid mass exceeds a certain mass concentration, leading to a slowdown in plume height expansion. However, at higher mass concentrations, the suspension's behavior becomes difficult to predict due to the complicated dynamics involved. Conventional models, which primarily account for the average drag exerted by particles, are insufficient in capturing the intricate interactions that occur at high mass concentrations. As a result, the reliance on empirical fit parameters becomes a limiting factor in understanding plume expansion in the presence of suspended particles. Moreover, the limitations of these models become even more apparent with non-spherical particles, which require further research and development to fully comprehend the underlying physics of plume expansion.

Over the past two decades, understanding the spread of epidemics within stochastic models has become a major research area. Most models assume that connections between individuals are random and bidirectional. However, some real-world scenarios involve directed interactions or group interactions that need to be considered. This study introduces a novel model that accounts for both directed interactions and group interactions using a hypergraph approach, where a set of individuals forms a connection through an edge, and an infection spreads through these edges. The model's parameters can be determined using the method of configuration type, and conditions are established for a mean-field phase transition and extinction based on the spectrum of the underlying network. These conditions apply to various special cases, including traditional 2-epidemics on complex networks and standard random networks.

Recent studies in recent years have intensified the investigation of two-dimensional (2D) magnetic substances which exhibit spin-orbit coupling. A particular class of 2D magnetic materials, characterized by Rashba-like spin-orbit coupling, is particularly captivating due to their unique properties. Despite the emergence of several 2D magnetic materials, a Rorschach-like drawing by Edvard Munch serves as a metaphor for the uncertainty surrounding these findings. Recent discovery of the phase transition between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic states in 2D CrI3 bilogues has opened new avenues for investigation, with CrI3 ferromagnetic state showing out-of-plane chirality. Furthermore, research into this ferromagnetic state has revealed complex interactions between the Rashba-like spin-orbit coupling and the material's intrinsic chirality. As an initial step in exploring this phenomenon, our study aims to analyze the electronic structure and spin-orbit interaction effects using Rashba-like models and the CrI3 atomic model as a concrete example. Utilizing a tight-binding model and incorporating techniques such as the Kohn-Sham method and full-potential linearized augmented plane-wave method, we find that the Rashba-like spin-orbit coupling significantly impacts the material's electronic structure and transport properties, with the research findings providing valuable insights for future exploration and potential applications.

The rotation of the Sun undergoes changes, yet details about solar-type star rotation remain unclear. By assuming K2f2h2-type differential rotation on stars with constant latitude-based shear, researchers developed magnetic cycles through numerical simulations, utilizing the P2LNL dynamo model. They discovered that stars with specific magnetic properties, particularly those exhibiting strong shear, exhibited enhanced dynamo efficiency and faster dynamo periods, predicting the existence of potential magnetic cycles in such stars, regardless of their overall rotation rate. However, predictions are challenging due to the lack of precise rotation rate and magnetic properties data. Understanding these factors is essential for determining the occurrence of magnetic cycles on magnetic, non-magnetic, and slowly rotating stars, which impacts our comprehension of planetary habitability and habitable zones.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable results in handling complex tasks, 
but they struggle with the integration of diverse input types like visual and text 
data due to the lack of a unified understanding of these inputs. Current methods 
for handling multimodal data are ineffective in cases where multiple inputs are 
related but distinct, resulting in poor performance and lost opportunities for 
cross-modal learning. This research presents a novel k-fan deep framework that 
can process multiple visual and text inputs in separate but interconnected pathways, 
enabling learning to adapt across various branches and a unified pathway to create 
a shared representation of all inputs. This approach was tested on the combined 
dataset of Caltech-60 and 345, as well as on data from the Google Image Search and 
Twitter, demonstrating significant performance enhancements and successful learning 
transfers across different network branches and a shared representation space.

The McMini model verifier generates test cases and validates programs by comparing the outcomes of a reference model and a program under test for both single and multi-threaded scenarios. For the latter, one prominent test generation technique is Delay-Prevention Ordering (DPOR), which yields both relevant and redundant events in threaded programs. Focusing on the fully dynamic McMini, improvements have been made to its DPOR implementation through support for indeterminate values, its handling is now a key research topic in both reduced and fully dynamic models.

In an effort to combat the spread of false information, WhatsApp has implemented measures to limit the ability of users to share messages. Specifically, the company added features in an update requiring users of the Android version of the app to log in to their WhatsApp accounts before they can share messages from news sources, while the iOS version already limits message sharing to a single share per source per day. These measures aim to slow the propagation of misinformation online and are expected to have a significant impact on how people share messages, especially in regions where WhatsApp dominates social media. Building on previous research, this study utilizes survey data from Germany and experimental data from a Twitter campaign in Israel to assess the effectiveness of these limitations. Our findings show that both features significantly reduce the speed at which messages are shared and spread across the network, and that significant portions of false information propagated online in the German elections may have been contained by the iOS sharing limit. Furthermore, one simulation demonstrates that a combination of the Android and iOS features could reduce the number of Germans exposed to the false claim that measles vaccines cause autism by a significant margin.

We analyze a branching population with non-infinite offspring and examine how a random sample of population members draws alleles from an ancestral population. The frequency of each allele in the sample is denoted as p. The probability distribution of these frequencies is examined, specifically how it varies with population size, is defined as f(p). The goal of our investigation is to determine how this prevalence spectrum, or Allele Frequency Spectrum (AFS), behaves and what properties it possesses.

This paper introduces an attentive activation mechanism designed to boost the effectiveness of spoof detection within end-to-end voice authentication systems. By incorporating this mechanism, spoofers are forced to provide additional proof of their identity beyond just their voice prints. We integrate the mechanism into a state-of-the-art spoofing detection system that employs spoof-agnostic features and exhibit its effectiveness on the ASV spoofing attack datasets. The approach achieves top performance in the IEEE CSPK challenge-2019, surpassing other methods including the incumbent system's baseline.

We've developed supersymmetric models of inflation that exhibit enhanced theoretical credibility. These models utilize a specific type of supergravity structure, which we use to follow the progress of inflation as it moves from one mathematical description to another, starting from an effective Field Theory of Inflation (EFTE) and eventually exiting with substantial density perturbations. Our analysis shows that even with significant fluctuations, the models remain within the range of validity for their underlying assumptions, confirming their efficiency. We also found that the primordial spectral index in these models falls within the range of current data from Planck but falls short of matching the results from the 2018 dataset analysis by Planck and the BICEP2/Keck dataset. Ultimately, our models provide a framework for constructing supersymmetric models of inflation with improved predictive accuracy.

When associated with a symmetry group in group theory, it makes sense to think of elements that don't fit this symmetry. In linear and quantum optics, elements associated with the unitary group include modes, states, beams, and sources, and when a unitary group acts on these components, their properties become clearer. However, this action also reveals aspects of the system that are inherently symmetric or asymmetric, and these characteristics become evident in experimental settings. Meanwhile, associations with the symplectic group also offer insights into the structure of quantum objects, and this exploration includes the generalization of the term "beams" in group theory, and the interpretation of experimental results in line with group actions.

Our experiment employs terahertz spectroscopy and near-field scanning to investigate the properties of superconducting microwave resonators and related quantum circuits. By using a nano-antenna and a nano-probe, we can spectroscopically analyze microwave modes and map their spatial distribution. Our results confirm that the terahertz spectroscopy spectroscopic results align with numerical simulations and provide insights into the operational properties of quantum circuits, making it a valuable tool for quantum technology characterization. The spatial mapping in the terahertz regime complements traditional microwave and optical methods, offering a new perspective on quantum devices. The proposed near-field scanning technique enhances sensitivity and improves spatial resolution, enabling a deeper understanding of quantum devices and potentially contributing to quantum technology development and troubleshooting.

We investigate the possibility of partitioning the real line into uncountably many sets, with each set containing a countable number of elements, all consisting of Borel sets. It is demonstrated that these sets can consist of analytic sets. However, it is established that uncountably many of these sets must consist of Lebesgue measurable sets, implying their divisibility into uncountably many sets, accessible through a choice principle and Martin's Axiom. We further examine specific properties of these sets, such as Baire measurability, Borel mapping preimages, and Lebesgue measurability. It is shown to be independent of set theory whether uncountably many of these sets, possessing specific mapping properties, have certain properties, such as being Borel or analytic sets.

In recent years, the adoption of machine learning in financial planning has been gradually increasing. To better comprehend the effects of this technique on current investment strategies, a simulation-based approach utilizing agent-based models was undertaken. These models enable the replication of various investment strategies in a virtual environment to assess the impact of integrating an agent representing techniques commonly associated with machine learning. Our results indicate that, based on specific assumptions regarding agent-based models, the incorporation of active trading strategies led to a significant decline in returns for all other strategies, including those not utilizing these methods, within the portfolio. Conversely, the integration of 'machine learning types' of traders had only a minimal effect on other strategies, suggesting a distinct investment approach. Moreover, we discovered that 'machine learning types' agents tend to enter and leave the market more rapidly than other strategies, which could indicate their limited suitability for traditional investment techniques.

This study explores vulnerabilities in the Protocol Analysis Module (PAM) of open-source network defense tools that perform protocol identification, a crucial function but subject to evasion by malicious traffic. An examination of PAM implementations across Scapy, Mininet, OpenFlow, and NetFlow reveals that most are susceptible to adaptive attacks, with only TensorFlow's TFFlow demonstrating robustness. To address this vulnerability, two novel machine learning models, including a multi-layer perceptron, are proposed and evaluated to outperform TFFlow. The research underscores the significance of developing resilient and trustworthy network security systems to safeguard critical network operations and to continue monitoring and assessing PAM modules to ensure the integration of reliable network defense tools.

We investigate the dynamics of thermal magnons in a ferromagnet under the influence of superconducting leads, with the goal of using superconductivity to control the thermal signal emitted by the magnons. We introduce a versatile theoretical framework for analyzing the magnon spectrum and transport properties arising from the complex interactions between the magnons, electrons, and superconducting leads. Our findings show that the proximity effect induces dissipation of thermal magnons via superconducting tunneling, thus dampening them and potentially isolating them. We isolate conditions under which this dissipation is minimal and dissipated magnons exhibit coherent behavior. We demonstrate that, within the proximity effect range, superconducting leads superpose a coherent magnon mode, which we propose could be used to strengthen the coupling between the magnons and external systems. We further demonstrate that the disordered magnon bath can be separated into two distinct parts, consisting of coherent and incoherent components, which can be used as a quantum hybrid system. We present a quantum optical model that illustrates the ability of superconducting leads to isolate the coherent magnon mode and thus function as a quantum filter that isolates quantum correlations from the environment's noise. We anticipate that the phenomena described here will open up new possibilities for quantum information processing through the integration of magnons and superconducting quantum technologies.

Audio classification has been extensively studied but current techniques are limited by large, well-annotated datasets which are difficult to obtain. This limitation is further exacerbated in the context of federated learning where audio data resides on individual user devices. Our proposed ZFLKA approach overcomes these obstacles by leveraging Google's Free Language Kinds Audio dataset and conducts extensive experiments comparing it with other methods, demonstrating the efficacy of our technique in achieving impressive results on challenging audio classification tasks.

There is a need for effective verification methods for multi-particle entangled quantum states. We identify a linear scaling formula, $E\approx 3dN$, for calculating the Bell inequalities in Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states of $N$ particles with $d$-level systems. Our analysis reveals that the Bell test could be more efficient than the quantum random access memory experiment. We suggest a more accessible approach involving automated and software-controlled operations to implement the Bell test. This is applicable to various scenarios such as testing high-dimensional continuous variables and performing automated tests in other experimental setups.

A Causal Estimation (CE) approach has been proposed to address the high reflectivity cause (SRC) and high transmission cause (HTC) in the context of Smart Reflecting Surface supported MultiUser MISO Frameworks. Traditional methods requiring non-causal estimates are inefficient and impractical, but our novel CE approach achieves optimal performance using only causal information. Our model utilizes a step-by-step backpropagation method to derive a closed-form efficient estimator for each reflectivity parameter. Furthermore, a related problem of estimating a maximum number of usable causes was also solved by transforming it into a solvable form and solving it optimally to guide the estimation process. Our technique surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and related cost (AC) efficiency by a significant margin and demonstrates remarkable performance at low signal-to-noise ratios while surpassing other cause estimation methods at low and high signal-to-noise ratios respectively in terms of a metric called the weighted sum mean-square error. Our results also demonstrate a remarkable gain in efficiency when using our technique versus the non-causal benchmark approach, resulting in substantial savings in resources and costs.

We examined connections between regional U.S. news consumption, local COVID-19 cases, deaths, and media audience behavior from February 2020 to March 2021. Using unit root and cointegration analysis on newspaper circulation data, we discovered that each region had a unique news landscape. When comparing overlapping and new stories, we found evidence of cointegration, indicating that media attention to the pandemic in each region was shaped by case and death rates. Specifically, we found a common pattern of cointegration between news and cases/deaths in three of the four regions. However, in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, circulation increased and cointegrated with cases and deaths. We observed consistent patterns within each region, but these patterns differed across regions, suggesting that understanding local news environments is crucial for understanding media-pandemic interactions.

The fundamental skill of counting is a crucial milestone in a child's cognitive development. 
Research has revealed that the acquisition of counting concepts is not linear but rather a combination of different strategies. 
To capture the nuances of counting progression, we developed an AI model incorporating Long Short-Term Memory and Gate Recurrent Neural Networks. 
This model was able to accurately simulate the patterns of typical children's counting behavior, including both warm-up and test sets. 
However, the model struggled to reproduce specific patterns exhibited by children with conceptual gaps, indicating a need for further investigation to better understand how the model processes information.

Bloom filters provide an approximate means of identifying elements within a set, with their reliability and size governed by the choice of hash functions. The well-established use of independent hash functions can be enhanced by replacing the exclusive or (xor) operation with more accurate element detection. Our solution retains hash functions, but without introducing new parameters, offering a more accurate detection mechanism. The elements of a set, when combined using the xor operation, do not necessarily result in zero, enabling improved filter accuracy. This concept is demonstrated with two variants - Or Filter and Sum Filter - each resulting in different outcomes depending on the operation employed, thereby outperforming traditional Bloom filters. Consequently, these filters can accurately identify set membership using fewer bits per element, ultimately enabling faster and easier application of digital circuit implementations.

This article explores connections between convex sets and analytic functions, 
focusing on two-dimensional results with a emphasis on illustrative examples and 
applications to the Carath\'{e}odory class.

To predict market trends, we must consider not only current data but also how past transactions impact future prices. This research focuses on uncovering market trend information from the sequence of market transactions, taking into account execution costs. We utilize a sequence extraction model, building upon the attention mechanism found in neural networks, to reflect the influence of execution costs on market trends. Furthermore, we develop multiple cost functions and train the model to simultaneously optimize extraction of market trends and optimization of returns in a multi-task learning scenario. This research also evaluates the model's ability to provide valuable investment decisions by comparing its performance to that of random investment strategies. The results show that the proposed market trend extraction model can effectively reflect the influence of execution costs and enable successful investments to be made by considering random strategies as a baseline for comparison.

Federated Learning (FL) is an emerging technology designed to preserve user privacy while training machine learning models distributed across multiple devices. Focusing on linear regression applications, we investigate the vulnerabilities of FL to data manipulation and malicious server behavior. Failing to account for uncertainties in Bayesian FL methods leads to potential abuses by FLVoogd, a discovered attack exploiting FL's weaknesses. We present several countermeasures to address FL's inherent vulnerabilities, enhancing their reliability without compromising privacy. Furthermore, we explore the feasibility of randomized response as a privacy preservation method, surpassing previous limits on accuracy within moderate privacy settings.

Achieving autonomous navigation in unfamiliar environments is a complex challenge due to the Sim2Real gap - the discrepancy between simulated and real-world conditions. Many research studies strive to overcome this gap by simulating diverse environments; however, the breadth of possible variations is vast, making it impractical to replicate every scenario in reality. This paper presents a novel approach to significantly reduce the Sim2Gap by capturing the directional cues present in both simulated and real-world images. Specifically, it demonstrates that leveraging the directional consistency found in visual features can significantly enhance the transition from simulation to reality. Moreover, this method enables the use of pre-trained image feature extractors to bridge the Sim2Gap, eliminating the need for complex multi-modal neural networks. Initially, this research focuses on a basic navigation task involving goal-directed movement. Although the proposed technique shows promising results in simulation, further evaluation is necessary to confirm its efficacy in real-world settings.

The advent of deepfake technology has fueled its widespread adoption, yet its abuse poses significant threats to privacy and can cause harm to individuals. To mitigate these risks, researchers and industry players strive to develop robust creation and detection methods. This article discusses several challenges in deepfake creation and detection due to content-specific and content-agnostic issues, and presents a unified framework for creating high-quality audio-visual deepfakes on any content with the accompanying identification methods. The proposed DeepFakeForge framework enables the generation of deepfakes using only two source videos, thereby eliminating the need for vast datasets. Furthermore, our framework can create high-quality deepfakes on any content, even those not used during training. Correspondingly, our proposed DeepFakeIdentify framework uses lightweight, discriminative models to accurately identify deepfakes in the audio-visual modality. Our methods have been evaluated on multiple public benchmarks, showcasing the superiority of the proposed frameworks over current state-of-the-art alternatives.

The detection of sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets exceeding 8.6 Earth masses, particularly those anticipated to have H2/He-dominated compositions, has led to a classification of "super-Submariners" as a new category of highly inflated planets. These planets, believed to contain internal "hot oceans" of water, have posed mysteries in understanding their anomalous inflation through observations of their atmospheric compositions and inflations. A theoretical model of these planets, based on the thermodynamic equilibrium between gas and condensed phases of water, hydrogensulfide, and ammonias, suggests a range of internal ocean depths and temperatures, which can be further explored through observations of the planet's transit signatures. The predictions of this model suggest that the variation in planet sizes among these sub-Neptune-sized planets may be a result of the different internal temperatures and compositions of these planets, which can be best understood through measurements of their atmospheric compositions and abundances. The future observations of these planets, such as the high-resolution spectroscopy of their atmospheres, may reveal the presence of internal ocean depths and temperatures, which would provide crucial insights into the planet's inflation mechanisms and formations.

Achieving complex pattern recognition in artificial neural networks is crucial for developing intelligent systems that can mimic human-like perception. Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) requires advanced learning capabilities beyond current machine learning frameworks. Neural networks with spiking neurons have the potential to overcome this challenge by leveraging their unique temporal and event-based properties to learn intricate patterns efficiently. Despite their high biological plausibility, overcoming the limitations of unsupervised learning in these networks has been a significant challenge until now. This work presents a significant breakthrough by introducing unsupervised learning of complex patterns in spiking neural networks, while maintaining biological feasibility. Our proposed method leverulates the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire model for neurons and uses Hebbian-based learning rules for weights and inhibitory connections, allowing the network to learn patterns efficiently and accurately. We further enhance this work by integrating global normalisation and side-inhibition mechanisms for better performance and robustness. Our results demonstrate the network's ability to learn patterns from unsupervised data of 2D shapes and colors, as well as 3D objects, without relying on detailed internal structure information. This research opens up new avenues for developing more advanced and efficient neural networks that can mimic human-like perception and cognition.

This report details the methods and results obtained from participating in
the out-of-distribution lexicon identification task of the 3rd Shared Task on
Multilingual and Cross-lingual NLP at NFeB 2021. Our approach involved training
two pre-established models on the full lexicon dataset, which were then employed
to generate predictions on the remaining test samples. The underlying idea was to
simulate a scenario where certain words are absent from the lexicon's training
phase. The derived predictions, along with two manually created baselines, were
submitted for evaluation. Notably, our primary model achieved the lowest error rate
and surpassed all benchmark performances.

A new approach combines the generalized polynomial chaos method with the reduced basis method to expand it beyond the limitations of Monte Carlo-based stochastic spectral methods. The proposed Laplace transform-based spectral expansion technique satisfies the Parallelogram Law, and we specifically utilize its finite dimension subspace property via the generalized PCE method. The stochastic Galerkin approach is employed to compute the exact Galerkin projection and an approximate projection is computed using the residual-based Laplace transform. The difference between these projections is measured to assess the approximation's quality. The generalized PCE method's ability to handle multivariate random inputs with various probability distribution functions makes it particularly suitable. The stochastic Galerkin approach is used to compute exact solutions for problems involving a random elastic plate and a stochastic quantum harmonic oscillator with random parameters. The approximation's quality is evaluated and the method's effectiveness is demonstrated in these examples.

This paper focuses on solving the complex issue of detecting and isolating changes in high-dimensional systems with many hidden variables. The problem arises in the context of manufacturing processes that have evolved over time but have limited knowledge of their current configurations. The proposed solution involves a two-step method that first identifies potential changes by monitoring the error of a predictive model trained on initial data. The method then alternates between taking data samples and refining the model to adapt to the new system dynamics, using algorithms designed for efficient learning. The second step employs statistical techniques to analyze local measurements and pinpoint the source of changes using a customized distance metric. The approach has been successfully tested on a real-world manufacturing system to demonstrate its practical applicability.

The study of compact dark matter halos, first envisioned by Zwicky in 1935, is pivotal for understanding the early universe's star formation, growth, and structure, particularly in predicting the early galaxy populations predicted by the Lambda CDM model. The first generation of galaxies, emerging within these halos, left behind traces in the present-day universe, which can be explored through the analysis of its stellar populations. By investigating these remnants, we can unlock information about the early universe, including the formation of the first galaxies. The satellite galaxies of the Milky Way, particularly those identified through the SDSS, serve as natural laboratories to study these ancient galaxies. The analysis of their populations and the compositions of their stars can provide valuable insights into the early universe's star formation and evolution. The second section will delve into the effects of these ancient galaxies on the early universe, focusing on the early galaxy populations' emergence within the first galaxies, which will be published in the third party's name.

Given a profinite group $G$, an action spectrum is a specific type of functor from G's continuous homotopy automorphisms to the category of simplicial sets. Existing action spectra are G-graded abelian groups, but new, non-abelian action spectra can be defined by utilizing properties of G-graded cohomology in a precise exact sequence. The action spectra formed in this manner constitute the entire set of action spectra, and they coincide with previously established action spectra when G is an abelian group. Additionally, action spectra for the profinite integers are shown to be in one-to-one correspondence with stochastic directed graphs.

Many organizations face difficulties in processing complex, visually-rich documents like invoices or legal papers, resulting in inaccurate machine-readable data due to their unique layouts and languages. In our research, we delve into the challenge of optical character recognition on visually intricate documents and the associated labeling costs. To address this, we introduce InvoFix, a state-of-the-art model for accurate OCR on visually complex invoices, paired with InvoFix-Lab, a labeling tool that minimizes human intervention by providing high-quality, pre-processed data to labelers, thus lowering expenses. Our study, spanning a wide range of invoice datasets, showcases InvoFix's exceptional performance, while InvoFix-Lab efficiently enhances the quality of labeled data, requiring just a basic understanding of data formatting. We've found that our model achieves a 44% higher labeling accuracy compared to standard OCR tools and only requires 10% human review for accurate labeling, effectively cutting labeling costs by 40%. For comparison, training robust OCR models from scratch demands 90% human oversight and 10 times more human resources than our model.

Our study on the interface between EuS and InAs is carried out with a detailed analysis of the electronic arrangement across the interfacial region through x-ray photoemission spectroscopy and first-principles calculations. By examining the spectral features of the Eu 4f electrons, we gain insight into the dependence of the electronic configuration on the specific alignment of EuS and InAs. Our analysis reveals that a complete transfer of the Eu 4f electrons' character from localized to band-like occurs only for EuS(001)-InAs(001) heterostructures, whereas other alignments exhibit an increased density of states within the energy gap, thus displaying an itinerant character. Furthermore, we discover that the charge transfer across the interfacial region leads to the formation of a small charge, approximately 0.05e, while our data also show that the charge distribution at the interface is highly sensitive to the specific alignment of EuS and InAs, exhibiting opposite signs for EuS(001)-InAs(00$\overline{1}$0) and EuS(001)-InAs(10$\overline{1}$0) alignments. Our research outcomes contribute valuable knowledge for the design and development of advanced spintronic and quantum devices built upon EuS materials.

This study expands the modular semantics for non-modal Lambek Calculi into a framework that integrates modal operators.  We focus on two types of modal operators: one representing potential (maybe) and another representing actuality.  We introduce two complete sound semantics and demonstrate that, when it comes to the modality of actuality, all modal languages based in Distributive Complete Lambek Calculi share uniform behavior.

The observation of neutron star - black hole collisions through gravitational waves is a pivotal area of study in astronomy, yet it is hindered by the limitations of current detectors, especially in the early phases of the event. A novel machine learning approach based on convolutional neural networks and a newly created dataset, OWL, overcomes these hurdles and enhances detection efficiency. The success of this method relies on distinctive patterns of gravitational waves generated during neutron star deformation, thereby illuminating crucial information about these events. The study emphasizes the importance of training data and suggests that pre-training on the Gravitational Wave Observatory dataset improves accuracy for the categorization of signals.

Our study focuses on a newly discovered exoplanet, TOI-5542 b, which is the 16th most distant, mass-radius indexed hot Jupiter known to date. Our analysis of Kepler data using various seizure detection algorithms revealed that TOI-5542 exhibits a genuinely periodic pattern. Subsequent stellar modeling utilizing Baumeister and APOORG codes shows that the star's properties are 079 solar masses, 063 solar radii, and approximately 4 billion years old. Utilizing chord modeling with a set of pre-established model atmospheres, our study indicates that TOI-5542 b has a radius of 1:32 Jupiter radii. The lack of observed transit signal beyond the main transit peak suggests that TOI-5542 b is likely not accompanied by large ring or satellite systems. This research explores a restricted version of Markov decision processes, 
where transitions are governed by a kernel that conditionally depends on states 
and actions through the equation $\mathbb{P}(\text{next state}|\text{current state, action}) = \int \text{next state}|\text{encodings of state and action} \cdot \pi$, 
with a goal to find an optimal policy and value function by maximizing value. 
It's proven that the original problem is tightly linked to a separately solvable 
optimized equation, enabling the development of two novel iterative algorithms 
that achieve optimal results. Furthermore, the research investigates how the 
optimal value function and its gradient are connected, leading to the creation 
of an innovative algorithm that achieves optimal convergence rates. 
These new methods offer improved alternatives to existing techniques, 
demonstrating their efficiency with a simple tabular test case.

Math is a fundamental component of scientific knowledge, its understanding is a marker of expertise.
Recognizing mathematical concepts offline, recognizing its importance in online systems, remains challenging due to its impact on accessibility.
Our solution combines state-of-the-art offline recognition systems with the interpretation of handwritten mathematics.
This solution offers individuals with math disabilities feedback and professionals, such as educators and medical practitioners, accurate diagnosis.
In addition, researchers benefit from validated hypotheses and scientists, including engineers and researchers, accurate finding results.
Our evaluation demonstrates that the proposed recognition system outperforms existing offline recognition systems on standard mathematical datasets.
The proposed recognition system utilizes R-Net and T-Net deep learning networks to recognize individual mathematical symbols and expressions separately.
These expressions are then combined using an HSMCR approach to determine the ultimate expression.
In contrast to existing deep learning-based offline recognition systems, our proposed system exhibits superior performance and exhibits improved robustness, especially in the detection of complex mathematical expressions containing fractions and variables raised to powers.

In this study, we investigate the endo-cohomology group of a specific sheaf that follows from the superpotential case of a four-dimensional N=2 super Yang-Mills theory with chiral multiplets, where we partially demonstrate that this cohomology group can be decomposed into a set of g+1 sheaf cohomology groups, each associated with an expansion of the Witten genus, which is further expressed in terms of Schur polynomials and elements of the Borel algebra. Notably, we observe that the time-dependent supersymmetric quantum constraint corresponds to the Cauchy-Riemann equation in the complex Borel algebra, leading to a connection between the cohomology group and the abstract expansion of the Witten genus, which is also linked to the Schubert classes. This connection is based on the work of Demazure and Manin. By examining a specific N=2 theory which arises from the N=1 four-dimensional theory proposed by Witten and extrapolated by Yau and Zhang, we were able to establish a direct relation between the cohomology group and the Schur polynomial through the superpotential. This work has its roots in the findings of Demazure and Manin.

This paper explores the concept of variability in network systems, utilizing a model based on the Firefly effect. We analyze how the average interaction time and its variation are interconnected with the system's overall structure, focusing on the relationships between these factors and the network variation system. By investigating the dynamics of the Firefly model, we are able to derive the recurrent equations for the system's statistical properties, allowing for the explanation of the observed correlations through the networks' structural characteristics. Notably, our research highlights the significance of the network's topology in determining the system's behavior, demonstrating how the diverse local environments within the networks give rise to diverse global behaviors.

Recent advancements in Reinforcement Learning agents, particularly those utilizing the Actor-Critic framework, have been significantly influenced by the integration of differentiable algorithms from External Differential Algorithms (EDAs). Notable examples include Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and MaxEnt-Policy Optimization (Max-Po), both of which framework-related approaches have similar goals, albeit through distinct methodologies. This study introduces a novel actor-critic method, Hamiltonian Actor-Critic (HAC), rooted in the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) method, an established technique in Reinforcement Learning value-based exploration. By incorporating novel insights into the Frank-Wolfe algorithm, HAC achieves a more efficient exploration process, resulting in enhanced sample efficiency and superior policy accuracy, particularly in Challenging Gym environments. Experimental evaluations have validated HAC's improved performance, demonstrating its reasonable computational cost and time requirements.
A fundamental proof of the well-known conjecture regarding frequent occurrence of prime numbers in close proximity has been conducted.

Recent breakthroughs in Deep Reinforcement Learning have made possible the development of efficient navigation strategies. However, integrating sonar data for navigation with Reinforcement Learning presents significant challenges. Sonar integration often involves time-consuming transformations and coordinate conversions that can impact training performance and sonar data availability during testing. To overcome these issues, we have designed a Stratified Navigation Controller, which fuses sonar data in a separate plane and applies the input directly to the agent's orientation and velocity outputs. Our research also involved comparing the performance of the Sonar input plane with traditional sonar integration methods and exploring the effects of different sonar parameters on the Sonar input plane. The results indicate that the Sonar input plane offers a promising approach, outperforming traditional methods while reducing computational load. The controller's simplicity also makes it highly versatile and applicable to a wide range of robotic platforms. Our open-source code is available on GitHub for verification and future research purposes.

We examine surfaces defined over specific sets of lower triangular matrices. These sets consist of $2\times2$ matrices over the real numbers with entries of the form $\begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}$, as well as $3\times3$ matrices with a similar structure but with zeros only in the upper right corner. These sets surface as the parameter spaces for certain affine and projective surfaces, specifically those linked to free lower triangular algebraic monoids and linear monoids, respectively. Our focus involves characterizing and describing the geometric features of these surfaces.

In the context of Bayesian dynamic treatment analysis, where the goal is to predict a patient's outcome based on a personalized treatment plan, it is essential to account for the uncertainty in treatment effects, especially since not all potential treatments are known at the time of decision-making. This uncertainty results in pessimistic predictions, reflecting the lowest guaranteed reward across all possible treatments. The current research develops Bayesian pessimistic values for decision-makers by first modeling uncertainty in outcome prediction using a Gaussian process and then defining pessimism as the minimum over all potential treatments. The pessimism minimization problem is challenging due to an infinite number of possible treatments, and the study resolves this by introducing an adaptive grid for treatments and approximating the minimum using the lowest pessimistic value at these points. The study shows that this approximation achieves consistent convergence and converges at the rate of $\sqrt{\log(1/h)/nh^2}$, where $n$ represents the number of historical patient data and $h$ denotes the grid spacing. The study compares a simple approximation method to more complex optimization techniques, such as linear and convex optimization, and demonstrates that this approach is sufficient without the need for more sophisticated methods. The study's approach incorporates the inherent Bayesian uncertainty in outcome modeling, and the resulting pessimistic values are validated using both synthetic and real-world healthcare data. The pessimism values perform well in comparison to other methods, and are particularly effective in scenarios characterized by sparse historical data and limited coverage.

Dualities in category theory serve as useful tools to increase understanding and resolve issues. This module guide will focus on key dualities that have proven effective in linear category and representation theory, notably the duality between tilting modules and support varieties, the equivalence between derived categories of tilting modules, and the relationship between cluster-tilting subcategories and cluster algebras. The aim is to provide concise summaries of these dualities, accompanied by examples and pointers to relevant literature. The guide will commence with an exploration of basic linear category principles.

A model is devised to examine the likelihood of quantum measurement outcomes from a complexification of the $E_8$ root system. This is achieved by defining complex roots with absolute value 1, resulting in projection operators with eigenvalues $\pm 1$. A set of 112 complex roots is identified, each associated with an octonion root. By combining the 112 octonion roots with 16 idempotent elements, a Hermitian O(16,16) vector with unit norm is formed, giving rise to a ray in a 32-dimensional real space. Furthermore, a corresponding O(16,16) weight vector exists within the $E_8$ real root space. It is demonstrated that the eigenvalues of Projector-based measurements along this O(16,16) weight vector direction are constrained by specific rational constraints. This projector corresponds to a 112-dimensional Hermitian and a 96-dimensional real symmetric matrix. This matrix structure was utilized to calculate the maximum violation of a specific inequality related to quantum entanglement distribution. A calculated maximum value of 132.42 lies in close proximity to the 99% confidence interval of an experiment involving 56 photons.
